會試錄序

皇明撫有六合，承平日久，天下士顒顒然咸有帝臣之願。其偕計集京師者，歲益以增。茲者又當會試，禮部籍數之，得四千人有奇。盖自洪武甲子定制開科，迄今適百年，凡三十有四舉矣。而人材之盛，前此未有踰於今日者。尚書臣洪謨、侍郎臣溥、臣一夔謹疏以聞。上命臣華、臣健司考校之柄，而同考臣遷、臣傑、臣臣、臣寬、臣希賢、臣瀚、臣孝、臣震、臣傑、臣昇、臣
translation_en:
Preface to the Metropolitan Examination Record

The august Ming dynasty holds sway over all within the six directions, and peace has long prevailed. Scholars throughout the realm earnestly aspire to become servants of the Emperor. Those who accompany the provincial delegations to assemble in the capital increase in number each year. Now that the Metropolitan Examination has again come due, the Ministry of Rites has registered and counted them, finding over four thousand men. From the jiazi year of the Hongwu reign [1384], when the regulations were established and examinations inaugurated, exactly one hundred years have now elapsed, during which thirty-four examinations have been held. Never before has the abundance of talent surpassed that of today.

Your servants Hongmo, Minister of Rites, and Pu and Yikui, Vice Ministers of Rites, respectfully submitted a memorial reporting this. His Majesty commanded your servants Hua and Jian to take charge of examining and evaluating the candidates, with Associate Examiners, your servants Qian, Jie, [name garbled: 臣臣, ?], Kuan, Xixian, Han, Xiao, Zhen, Jie, Sheng, and your servant …

title: 成化二十年會試錄
text:
聰臣洵臣明臣文卿監試臣瑄
臣璧暨内外諸執事咸遴選
以充臣等奉
命唯謹拔其尤者僅得三百人
遵
聖斷也於是列諸執事及中式氏
名幷擇其文刻諸梓以獻而
昭示永久華竊惟古稱治世
莫盛於唐虞三代以其政敎
出於一故也三代而下治則
雜矣我
國家
列聖相承純以堯舜禹湯文武周
孔之道理天下自國都及郡
alt_text:
聽臣洵臣明臣文卿監試臣宣
臣壁暨內外諸執事咸遴選
以充臣等奉
命唯謹拔其尤者僅得三百人
遵
聖斷也於是列諸執事及中式氏
名并擇其文刻諸梓以獻而
===
昭示永久華竊惟古稱治世
莫盛於唐虞三代以其政教
出於一故也三代而下治則
雜矣我
國家
列聖相承純以堯舜禹湯文武周
孔之道理天下自國都及郡
punctuated:
聰、臣洵、臣明、臣文卿，監試臣瑄、臣璧暨内外諸執事，咸遴選以充。臣等奉命唯謹，拔其尤者，僅得三百人，遵聖斷也。於是列諸執事及中式氏名，幷擇其文，刻諸梓以獻，而昭示永久。
華竊惟古稱治世，莫盛於唐虞三代，以其政敎出於一故也。三代而下，治則雜矣。我國家列聖相承，純以堯舜禹湯文武周孔之道理天下，自國都及郡
translation_en:
…Cong, your servants Xun, Ming, and Wenqing; the examination supervisors, your servants Xuan and Bi; and all the functionaries from within and outside the capital were carefully selected to fill their posts. We, your servants, carried out the command with the utmost care, selecting the most outstanding candidates and obtaining just three hundred, in accordance with Your Majesty’s decision. We thereupon listed the names of all the functionaries and successful candidates, selected their examination essays, and had these cut on printing blocks for presentation to the throne and for public instruction for all time.
I, Hua, humbly reflect that among the well-governed ages praised in antiquity, none surpassed those of Tang and Yu and the Three Dynasties, because their government and moral instruction issued from a single source. After the Three Dynasties, governance became mixed. In our dynasty, successive sagely sovereigns have governed all under Heaven solely through the Way of Yao, Shun, Yu, Tang, Kings Wen and Wu, the Duke of Zhou, and Confucius. From the national capital to the prefectures…

title: 成化二十年會試錄
text:
縣莫不設學以居俊秀之子
弟而學焉者專之以易書詩
春秋禮樂之經會之以論語
大學中庸孟子之書翼之以
周程張朱諸大儒之說秦漢
以来衆技百家者流一切黜
而不講至於三年一大比自
===
===
鄉舉升于禮部禮部舉而進
于
大廷惟經術焉是取隋唐以来
明法字算秀才童子諸科詩
賦墨帖浮艶淺陋之習一切
罷而不用夫所以居之者無
異所教之者無異術取之者

punctuated: 縣，莫不設學，以居俊秀之子弟。而學焉者，專之以《易》《書》《詩》《春秋》《禮》《樂》之經，會之以《論語》《大學》《中庸》《孟子》之書，翼之以周、程、張、朱諸大儒之說。秦漢以来衆技百家者流，一切黜而不講。至於三年一大比，自鄉舉升于禮部，禮部舉而進于大廷，惟經術焉是取。隋唐以来明法、字算、秀才、童子諸科，詩賦墨帖浮艶淺陋之習，一切罷而不用。夫所以居之者無異所，教之者無異術，取之者
translation_en: …counties, schools have been established everywhere to accommodate talented young men. Those studying there concentrate on the classics of Changes, Documents, Odes, Spring and Autumn Annals, Rites, and Music; bring their learning together through the Analects, Great Learning, Doctrine of the Mean, and Mencius; and supplement it with the teachings of the great Confucian scholars Zhou, Cheng, Zhang, and Zhu. The various specialized arts and schools of thought that have circulated since the Qin and Han are all excluded from instruction. As for the great examination held every three years, those selected in the Provincial Examination advance to the Ministry of Rites, and those selected by the Ministry of Rites proceed to the imperial court. Only learning in the Confucian classics is used as the basis for selection. The examination categories instituted since the Sui and Tang—Understanding the Law, Characters and Calculation [?], Cultivated Talent, and Child Prodigy—and the florid, superficial practices of verse, rhapsodies, and written recitation of textual passages [?] have all been abolished and are no longer used. Thus, there are no differing institutions in which they are educated, no differing methods by which they are taught, and, in selecting them …

title: 成化二十年會試錄
text:
無異途宜乎士有定志而無
異業爭自濯磨以待
國家之用者肩相摩踵相接其
盛臻兹哉嗟乎士之進取者
濟濟如此而有司所拔曾不
及什一何也重其選也諸士
子既與兹選旬日入奉
清問漸膺職任之寄盍思所以
毋負哉士窮居常恨不見用
及用矣或曰我位猶卑位尊
志得矣又或淫於貴富而盡
棄其平生此庸眾人猶或薄
之
國家所以待士者何如而士肯

清閟漸膺職任之寄盡思所以
毋負哉士窮居常恨不見用
及用矣或曰我位猶卑位尊
志得矣又或淫於貴富而盡
棄其平生與庸衆人猶或薄
之
國家所以待士者何如而士肯
punctuated: 無異途。宜乎士有定志而無異業，爭自濯磨以待國家之用者，肩相摩，踵相接，其盛臻兹哉！嗟乎！士之進取者濟濟如此，而有司所拔曾不及什一，何也？重其選也。諸士子既與兹選，旬日入奉清問，漸膺職任之寄，盍思所以毋負哉！士窮居，常恨不見用；及用矣，或曰：「我位猶卑。」位尊志得矣，又或淫於貴富，而盡棄其平生。此庸眾人猶或薄之。國家所以待士者何如，而士肯
translation_en: …there are no different avenues. It is fitting, then, that scholars should have a settled purpose and pursue no other occupation. Those who vie to refine and polish themselves in readiness for service to the state stand shoulder to shoulder and heel to heel. Such flourishing has now been attained! Alas! Those scholars seeking advancement are so numerous, yet those selected by the responsible officials do not amount even to one in ten. Why is this? Because selection is treated as a matter of utmost importance. Now that you scholars have been included in this selection, in ten days you will enter the imperial presence to receive His Majesty’s questions, and gradually be entrusted with official responsibilities. Should you not consider how to avoid betraying that trust? Scholars living in straitened circumstances constantly lament that they are not employed. Once employed, some say, “My rank is still low.” When their rank is high and their ambitions fulfilled, some become engrossed in wealth and distinction and utterly abandon their lifelong commitments. Even ordinary people may disdain such conduct. Considering how the state treats its scholars, could scholars be willing to…

title: 成化二十年會試錄
text:
以此自處乎夫士之仕也將
以行其學也事
君理民之道具載諸經在舉而措
之耳奚假於外求哉夙興夜
寐仰則聖謨一心一德不奪
不移補
袞職於
===
===
朝廷霈膏澤於黎庶企前烈引
後賢共弼成唐虞三代之盛
治庶下不負所學上不負
作育簡拔之恩維
皇明享有無疆之休諸君子亦永
有無窮之譽嗚呼其念之哉
成化二十年春二月壬午

作育簡拔之恩維
皇明享有無疆之休諸君子亦永
有無窮之譽嗚呼其念之哉
成化二十年春二月壬午
punctuated:
以此自處乎？夫士之仕也，將以行其學也。事君理民之道，具載諸經，在舉而措之耳，奚假於外求哉？夙興夜寐，仰則聖謨，一心一德，不奪不移，補袞職於朝廷，霈膏澤於黎庶，企前烈，引後賢，共弼成唐虞三代之盛治，庶下不負所學，上不負作育簡拔之恩。維皇明享有無疆之休，諸君子亦永有無窮之譽。嗚呼，其念之哉！
成化二十年春二月壬午。
translation_en:
…conduct themselves in this way? A scholar enters office in order to put his learning into practice. The principles of serving the ruler and governing the people are fully recorded in the Classics; one need only take them up and apply them. What need is there to seek elsewhere? Rise early and retire late, reverently model yourselves on the sage counsels, and remain united in purpose and virtue, neither diverted nor swayed. Remedy shortcomings in the sovereign’s discharge of his duties at court, and shower blessings upon the common people. Aspire to the achievements of your predecessors and bring forward worthy successors. Together, help bring about flourishing government like that of Tang and Yu and the Three Dynasties. Thus may you prove worthy, below, of your learning and, above, of the gracious favor shown in nurturing and selecting you. May the august Ming enjoy boundless blessings, and may you gentlemen likewise possess enduring and inexhaustible renown. Ah, take this to heart!
The renwu day of the second month, spring, in the twentieth year of Chenghua [1484].

translation_en:
Metropolitan Examination of the Twentieth Year of Chenghua (1484)

Chief Administrators of the Examination

Xu Pu, Grand Master for Thorough Counsel, Left Vice Minister of Rites and concurrently Academician of the Hanlin Academy. His courtesy name was Shiyong; he was from Yixing County in Zhili and was a metropolitan graduate (jinshi) of the jiaxu year.

Xie Yikui, Grand Master for Thorough Counsel and Right Vice Minister of Rites. His courtesy name was Dashao; he was from Xinjian County in Jiangxi and was a metropolitan graduate of the gengchen year.

Examiners

Peng Hua, Grand Master for Thorough Counsel, Supervisor of the Household in the Household Administration of the Heir Apparent and concurrently Academician of the Hanlin Academy. His courtesy name was Yanshi; he was from Anfu County in Jiangxi and was a metropolitan graduate of the jiaxu year.

title: 成化二十年會試錄
text:
第壹場
四書
人能弘道非道弘人
是故君子戒慎乎其所不睹恐懼乎其所
不聞
物皆然心為甚
易
直方大不習无不利則不疑其所行也
聖人亨以享上帝而大亨以養聖賢
===
富有之謂大業日新之謂盛德
仰則觀象於天俯則觀法於地觀鳥獸之
文與地之宜近取諸身遠取諸物於
是始作八卦
書
帝乃誕敷文德舞干羽于兩階七旬有苗
格
各守爾典以承天休爾有善朕弗敢蔽
其作大邑其自時配皇天毖祀于上下其

問：三代之制，至周而大備。武王末受命，其所以斟酌前代之制而鉅細畢舉者，大抵皆周公為之。繼周而治、享國長久者，曰漢，曰唐，曰宋。其創業之君在位日淺，未及規畫久安長治之策，凡其法制有可稱者，率多繼世者之所定也。惟我太祖高皇帝，取天下於腥羶之餘，復綱常於淪斁之後，而其所以規畫為萬世典則者，至精至密，可以世世行之而無弊，三代以來所未有也。今其訓誥律令制詔諸書具在，諸士子蓋亦嘗莊誦矣。請悉其典則之善，用示夫日用而不知者。

Counterfeiting paper currency.
Illicitly breaching river embankments.

Third Session. Five policy questions.

Question: The institutions of the Three Dynasties reached their fullest development under the Zhou. King Wu received the Mandate late in life [?]; the work of weighing the institutions of preceding dynasties and establishing every provision, great and small, was largely done by the Duke of Zhou. Among the dynasties that ruled after the Zhou and endured for a long time were the Han, Tang, and Song. Their founding rulers reigned only briefly and had no time to devise plans for lasting peace and enduring good government. Whatever was commendable in their laws and institutions was generally established by their successors.

Our Emperor Taizu Gao alone won the realm in the aftermath of rule by those who reeked of meat and mutton, and restored the cardinal human relationships and constant moral principles after their collapse and corruption. The standards and precedents he devised for all ages were supremely refined and thorough, capable of being implemented generation after generation without ill effect—an achievement unprecedented since the Three Dynasties. His books of admonitions, proclamations, statutes, ordinances, and imperial decrees are all extant, and you candidates have presumably read them reverently. Set forth fully the excellence of these standards and precedents, so as to enlighten those who follow them daily without understanding them.

translation_en:
Question: From antiquity, rulers of all under Heaven who wished to rectify customs and make moral instruction effective needed only a court capable of employing worthy men and scholar-officials capable of maintaining their integrity. Yet the court’s employment of worthy men depends upon impartial channels of recommendation, while scholar-officials’ maintenance of their integrity depends upon a clear understanding of moral principles. Each thus has its foundation. In the flourishing ages of Tang and Yu and the Three Dynasties, no worthy men remained overlooked outside office, and scholars held steadfast principles. These two achievements are certainly difficult to equal. For now, let us discuss the Han and Tang and subsequent times. Their outstanding and righteous rulers sometimes sought counsel throughout the realm and promoted its most gifted men; sometimes discussed the Six Classics and recruited men of exceptional ability; sometimes honored righteousness, cherished worthy men, and acted upon loyal counsel; and sometimes appointed men with care and held their chief ministers responsible for results. They may be said to have been capable of employing worthy men. But were the channels of recommendation in those times truly impartial in every respect?

Among their worthy scholar-officials, some alone offered the General-in-Chief a bow with clasped hands; some declined appointment as Remonstrance Grandee; some were content to withdraw into quiet retirement and did not attend examinations at court, or felt ashamed to pass judgment on upright men and never again presented themselves for examination; and some regarded visiting princes and dukes as selling themselves, and assiduously attending to official duties as seeking recognition. They may be said to have been capable of maintaining their integrity. But was their understanding of moral principles truly clear in every respect? Examining fairly the moral instruction and customs of these several dynasties, we must also ask whether they could truly match the flourishing ages of Tang and Yu and the Three Dynasties.

問井田之制有阡陌以經界有溝澮以畜
punctuated:
庶位皆賢，而士能有守。然而僥倖之徒猶存，奔競之風未息，豈薦舉之途未盡公、義理之學未盡明歟？抑别有其故歟？兹欲使朝廷之上賢才充滿，而僥倖者難容；士大夫之間廉耻興行，而奔競者自息，果何道以致之歟？諸士子博通古今，必有至當之論，願明著于篇。

問：秦漢而下，儒之醇者莫如宋，而宋儒之醇莫如周程張朱四子。周子嘗作《太極圖》，張子嘗作《西銘》，尤其言之醇者也。而或詆其為老氏之宗旨，或疑其同墨氏之兼愛，果何所據歟？當時所謂醇儒者，固嘗為之力辯矣，而或從或否，至于今猶不能無惑焉。夫吾儒之於老墨，不啻氷炭，毫釐之差，千里之謬。諸士子皆以儒名，其折諸理，一一辯之，毋膠於偏見。

問：井田之制，有阡陌以經界，有溝澮以畜
translation_en:
…all offices should be occupied by worthy men, and scholars should be able to uphold their principles. Yet those seeking advancement through undeserved good fortune still remain, and the practice of scrambling for office has not ceased. Is this because the channels of recommendation are not entirely impartial, or because the learning of moral principles has not been fully elucidated? Or is there some other cause? We now wish to see the court filled with worthy talent, leaving little room for those seeking undeserved advancement, and integrity and a sense of shame flourishing among scholar-officials, so that scrambling for office ceases of itself. By what means can this truly be achieved? You candidates possess broad knowledge of past and present and must have thoroughly sound arguments. Please set them out clearly in your essays.

Question: From the Qin and Han onward, no Confucian scholars surpassed those of the Song in doctrinal purity; among the Song scholars, none surpassed the four masters Zhou, Cheng, Zhang, and Zhu. Master Zhou composed the Diagram of the Supreme Ultimate (Taiji tu), and Master Zhang composed the Western Inscription (Xi ming), works especially exemplary of the purity of their teachings. Yet some have disparaged the former as expressing the central doctrine of Laozi, while others have suspected the latter of being identical to Mozi’s doctrine of impartial care. What grounds do these claims actually have? Those regarded at the time as Confucian scholars of pure doctrine certainly defended these works vigorously. Yet some accepted their arguments and others did not, and even today doubts persist. Our Confucian teachings and those of Laozi and Mozi are as incompatible as ice and burning charcoal: a discrepancy of a hair’s breadth leads to an error of a thousand miles. You candidates all bear the name of Confucian scholars. Judge these matters by principle and distinguish them one by one; do not cling to partial views.

Question: Under the well-field system, there were paths running lengthwise and crosswise to demarcate the fields, and ditches and channels to retain…

title: 成化二十年會試錄
text:
洩先王養民之大政也然特行於江漢
以北平衍之地耳自秦開阡陌盡地力
於是先王之制蕩廢殆盡而秦益以富
强及漢有天下因秦之舊而穀粟之豐
財用之饒出於北者自若也豈開阡陌
誠利邪抑先王之遺澤猶有存邪迨吳
晉以後財賦漸盛於東南至于有宋而
數倍於北矣今
朝廷之所需百官之所資率於東南乎取之
===
而西北殆不及什一則所謂廢井田以
富國者安在其為富也且不獨不足以
供
國用而已一遇水旱則嗷嗷待哺至遣朝臣
發內帑以賑貸之猶不免於轉徙夫今
之地猶古之地今之民猶古之民也而
其不同有如此經國者宜有以區處之豈
可徒委之氣數邪諸生於天下事展轉
於心久矣茲將出而有官守之寄其明

translation_en:
…and discharge water: this was a great policy by which the former kings sustained the people. Yet it was practiced only on the broad, level lands north of the Changjiang and Han rivers. When Qin opened up the field boundaries and fully exploited the productive capacity of the land, the institutions of the former kings were swept away almost entirely, while Qin became still wealthier and stronger. When Han gained possession of the realm, it continued Qin’s arrangements, and the abundant grain and ample fiscal resources supplied by the north remained as before. Was opening up the field boundaries truly beneficial? Or did some of the beneficent legacy of the former kings still survive?

From the Wu and Jin periods onward, fiscal revenues gradually grew more abundant in the southeast; by the Song period, they were several times those of the north. Today, the court’s requirements and the resources supporting the officials are largely drawn from the southeast, while the northwest supplies scarcely one-tenth as much. Where, then, is the enrichment supposedly achieved by abolishing the well-field system to enrich the state? Nor is it merely that the northwest cannot supply the state’s needs. Whenever flood or drought strikes, its people cry out for food. Even when court officials are dispatched to release funds from the palace treasury for relief grants and loans, the people still cannot avoid displacement and migration.

The land today is still the land of antiquity, and the people today are still the people of antiquity, yet the difference in their circumstances is so great. Those who administer the state ought to devise ways of addressing this. How can they simply attribute it to the cycles of cosmic forces and fate? You candidates have long turned the affairs of the realm over in your minds. Now you are about to enter service and be entrusted with official responsibilities. You should clearly…

者何如耳大舜敷文德而格有苗載諸

translation_en:
…and thereby inform the responsible officials.

Question: The peoples beyond the frontiers have troubled the Central Kingdom since antiquity; the issue is simply how to defend against them. The great Shun spread civil virtue and thereby brought the Youmiao to submission, as recorded in the Book of Yu. King Xuan deployed his great war chariots and attacked the Xianyun, as set forth in the Odes of Zhou. Thus, even under Yu and Zhou, their methods of resisting these peoples differed to this extent. In later ages, Emperor Wu of Han repelled the peoples of the four quarters and expanded his territory by a thousand li; Emperor Taizong of Tang destroyed the northern foes, and his armies suffered neither defeat nor rout. Their military successes were unmatched by earlier ages, yet some critics censured them for wanton warfare. From the decline of Tang onward, the frontier peoples grew powerful and overbearing. The Song could not subdue them and sent gold and silk annually to establish peaceful relations, but critics faulted this as seeking peace merely for the moment. Then our Taizu drove out the alien Yuan and pacified the realm, achieving deeds surpassing those of the emperors and kings of antiquity. Yet today, after a long period of peace and ease, remnants of the enemy appear and disappear unpredictably. Although their numbers are reckoned at less than one hundredth of those of the Central Kingdom, the trouble they cause along the frontier has never been quelled. Should we send gold and silk to secure their friendship? That certainly would not uphold the dignity of the Central Kingdom. Or should we exhaust our military resources to overawe them? We fear, however, that this would mean wanton warfare and suffering for the people. We must deter them with might without resorting to wanton warfare, and win their allegiance through kindness without becoming unduly familiar, so that the frontier peoples retreat into hiding and the borderlands enjoy peace. 日之利宜以對毋諉曰未之學也

punctuated: 九重之所欲聞者。願考古人之得失，而陳今日之利宜以對，毋諉曰：「未之學也。」
translation_en: …is what His Majesty wishes to hear. Examine the successes and failures of the ancients and, in your response, set forth what would be beneficial and appropriate today. Do not evade the question by saying, “I have not studied this.”

title: 成化二十年會試錄
text:
第壹場
四書
人能弘道非道弘人
朱攴
同考試官郎中陳批體認真切必刻意於
理學者
同考試官編修劉批題本難作場中窘筆
宜矣此篇鋪敘明白說得弘字是故錄之
考試官庶子劉批詞順意足
===
考試官學士彭批語不冗雜
人能大所具之理理不能大所寓之人蓋道者
人所具之理也人於所具之理則能大之而其
理豈能以自大哉何則道之大原雖出於天而
其實則具於人人外無道道外無人有不可得
而離者然人心有覺而道體無為故人於道則
能大之而道豈能大乎人哉如父子之親君臣
之義道也夫婦之别長幼之序朋友之信亦道
也人於是道自其日用之間而廓之可以位天

人能大所具之理，理不能大所寓之人。蓋道者，人所具之理也。人於所具之理則能大之，而其理豈能以自大哉？何則？道之大原雖出於天，而其實則具於人。人外無道，道外無人，有不可得而離者。然人心有覺，而道體無為，故人於道則能大之，而道豈能大乎人哉？如父子之親、君臣之義，道也；夫婦之别、長幼之序、朋友之信，亦道也。人於是道，自其日用之間而廓之，可以位天
translation_en:
First Session
Four Books
“A person can broaden the Way; it is not the Way that broadens the person.”
Zhu Pu 朱攴 [?]
Associate Examiner Chen, Director, comments: “His understanding is genuine and penetrating. He must be someone who applies himself earnestly to the study of principle.”
Associate Examiner Liu, Compiler, comments: “The topic is inherently difficult to write on, so difficulty in composing an answer in the examination hall is only to be expected. This essay develops its exposition clearly and explains the word ‘broaden’ correctly; hence its selection.”
Examiner Liu, Vice Supervisor of Instruction, comments: “The language flows smoothly, and the meaning is fully expressed.”
Examiner Peng, Academician, comments: “The language is neither verbose nor cluttered.”
A person can enlarge the principle with which he is endowed; principle cannot enlarge the person in whom it resides. For the Way is the principle with which a person is endowed. A person can enlarge the principle within him, but how could that principle enlarge itself? Why is this so? Although the great source of the Way issues from Heaven, its substance is present within human beings. Outside human beings there is no Way; outside the Way there are no human beings. The two cannot be separated. Yet the human mind has awareness, while the substance of the Way does not act. Thus a person can enlarge the Way, but how could the Way enlarge a person? The affection between father and son and the righteousness between ruler and minister are the Way. The distinction between husband and wife, the order between elder and younger, and trustworthiness between friends are also the Way. If a person extends this Way in the course of everyday life, he can set Heaven …

title: 成化二十年會試錄
text:
地而育萬物以極乎功化之盛焉自其常行之
際而充之可以參天地而贊化育以極乎功用
之大焉人能大其道如此而道之為體也雖曰
蟠際于天地然斂之方寸而寂然無為豈能大
其人而自行於日用之間乎雖曰充塞乎宇宙
然藏之一心而冲漠無朕豈能大其人而自見
於常行之際乎是則人也道也原其實固非有
二然所以廓大之任當責之人而道豈能與哉
抑又論之人禀天地之理氣而生氣以為之形
===
理以為之性合理與氣而有覺為之心是性乃
所以生之理而心則主此形統此性者也故張
子釋此章以心能盡性為人能弘道惟不知檢
其心為非道弘人學者合而味之聖人之意益
于是而可見
是故君子戒慎乎其所不睹恐懼乎其所
不聞
儲巏
同考試官給事中仰批 理有定見語無

地而育萬物，以極乎功化之盛焉；自其常行之際而充之，可以參天地而贊化育，以極乎功用之大焉。人能大其道如此，而道之為體也，雖曰蟠際于天地，然斂之方寸而寂然無為，豈能大其人而自行於日用之間乎？雖曰充塞乎宇宙，然藏之一心而冲漠無朕，豈能大其人而自見於常行之際乎？是則人也，道也，原其實固非有二，然所以廓大之任當責之人，而道豈能與哉？抑又論之，人禀天地之理氣而生，氣以為之形，理以為之性，合理與氣而有覺為之心。是性乃所以生之理，而心則主此形、統此性者也。故張子釋此章，以心能盡性為人能弘道，惟不知檢其心為非道弘人。學者合而味之，聖人之意益于是而可見。
是故君子戒慎乎其所不睹，恐懼乎其所不聞。

translation_en:
…and Earth in their proper places and nurture the myriad things, thereby bringing the transforming efficacy of his achievement to its fullest flourishing. By extending it through his ordinary conduct, he can stand alongside Heaven and Earth and assist their transforming and nurturing work, thereby bringing its practical efficacy to its greatest extent. Such is a person’s ability to enlarge his Way. Yet as for the Way itself, although it is said to extend throughout Heaven and Earth, it is gathered within the heart, still and inactive. How could it enlarge the person and put itself into practice in daily life? Although it is said to fill the universe, it is stored within a single mind, utterly tranquil and without perceptible trace. How could it enlarge the person and manifest itself in ordinary conduct? Thus, when we trace person and Way to their underlying reality, they are certainly not two separate things. Nevertheless, responsibility for expanding and enlarging the Way must be laid upon the person. How could the Way itself undertake it?
To discuss this further: a person is born endowed with the principle and material force of Heaven and Earth. Material force constitutes his bodily form, and principle constitutes his nature. The union of principle and material force, possessing awareness, constitutes his mind. This nature is the principle by which he lives, while the mind governs his bodily form and commands his nature. Thus Master Zhang, in explaining this passage, took the mind’s capacity fully to realize human nature as the meaning of “A person can enlarge the Way,” and the failure to examine one’s own mind as the meaning of “It is not the Way that enlarges the person” [?]. If students consider these explanations together and ponder them, the sage’s meaning will become all the clearer.
“Therefore the gentleman is watchful and cautious concerning what he does not see, and fearful and apprehensive concerning what he does not hear.”

…at the moment when no affair has yet called forth a response, there is also that which one does not hear. When the ears hear nothing, how could one allow even the slightest slackening? The gentleman’s heart remains vigilant, always preserving fear and apprehension. At such a moment, although he hears not a single matter, he still dares not slacken in the least. Not seeing and not hearing belong to stillness, before feelings have been aroused; yet the gentleman’s reverence and awe remain uninterrupted in this way. Thus he preserves Heavenly principle in its original state and does not allow himself to depart from it even for an instant. How essential is this effort to embody the Way! Nor is this all: the following passage also speaks of the gentleman being watchful over himself when alone, which is another essential aspect of self-examination. In stillness, he maintains reverence to preserve and nourish his heart; in activity, he maintains reverence to examine it. In activity and stillness alike, his heart is never without reverence, and he never departs from the Way. Is this not why the gentleman’s effort to embody the Way lies beyond the reach of ordinary people?

“This Is So with All Things, but Especially with the Heart”
Wang Qiong 王瓊

Things differ, and must indeed be measured with instruments; the heart’s responses are even harder to bring into proper proportion, and must especially be measured against principle. Things have weight and length, which become apparent only after measurement with instruments. As for the heart’s responses to things, the difficulty of bringing their relative weight and extent into proper proportion exceeds even that of external things. How, then, could one fail to measure them against the principle inherent in the heart? Formerly, because the King of Qi extended his kindness to birds and beasts, yet its benefits did not reach the common people, Mengzi instructed him in these terms. His meaning was this: all things under Heaven have relative weight and length. Only by weighing them on a balance can one know which are light and which heavy. This is certainly not true of just one thing. Although the myriad things differ, could anyone know their weight without a balance? Only by measuring them with a measure of length can one know which are long and which short. This is certainly not true of just one thing. Although the myriad things are diverse, could anyone know their length without a measure?
If this is so even for external things that require measurement, how much more must it be so for the heart, the master of the whole person! Its responses to things likewise have relative weight and extent. If I do not use the principle inherent in my heart as their balance, I will give little weight to what should be weighty and great weight to what should be light, failing to accord each its due. If I do not use the principle inherent in my heart as their measure of length, I will extend what should be limited and limit what should be extended…

…and thus fails to accord with the mean. Things have form, so it is easy to measure their weight and length. Without scales and measures, the error concerns no more than a single thing. The mind has no form, so it is difficult to measure its weight and length. If the mind lacks scales and measures, a discrepancy of a hair’s breadth leads to an error of a thousand miles. How could this amount merely to a mistake in a single affair? Thus the need to measure the mind is even greater than the need to measure things. The King of Qi’s concern for creatures was weighty and far-reaching, while his benevolence toward the people was slight and limited. He had lost the scales and measures inherent in his mind without knowing it. This is why Mengzi instructed him in these terms; his intention was profound indeed. Generally speaking, everyone’s good heart manifests itself at some moment. The King of Qi’s inability to bear the ox’s trembling with fear was just such a manifestation. But once selfish intentions arise, people often do what they would otherwise refuse to do and endure what they would otherwise find unbearable. Mengzi drew upon what the king understood to assail what obscured his understanding, earnestly urging him to extend his kindness to the common people. He may well be called adept at guiding a ruler onto the proper Way. Alas, the King of Qi could not extend this kindness and put it into practice!

When virtue is complete and action brings favorable results, one has no doubts in dealing with affairs. Those who have doubts must practice before they can obtain favorable results. The noble man possesses the virtues of straightness, squareness, and greatness and faces affairs without doubt; thus, wherever he goes, nothing is unfavorable. Why should he need further practice? In the Commentary on the Words of the Text, the sage develops the meaning of the Commentary on the Images for the second, yin line of Kun, explaining it in terms of learning. Straightness, squareness, and greatness are the virtues of Kun. If the noble man can learn, these virtues reside not merely in Kun but in the noble man himself.

Consequently, without awaiting study and practice, he applies this to his undertakings, and naturally nothing is unfavorable. 其藏諸用者而言之凡物之洪纖高下孰不具

无一物而不具造化之理不含造化之性則无
一物非造化之所成矣造化之所成富有如此
凡業之成於外者孰能過之此其所以為大業
歟自其顯諸仁者而言之物既无一不具造化

生之機或已化化之妙則无一理非造化之所

孰能踰之此其所以為盛德歟吁業焉而大德
焉而盛天地之所以无心而成化者于是見矣
抑大傳此章前既以盛德大業為言至此乃先
言業而後言德者蓋以造化之序言之固理先

相承相禪於无窮不然則理无所寓而造化或

Speaking of what is concealed in their functioning, among all things, great and small, high and low, which does not embody the principle of creation and transformation? Among creatures that fly, swim, crawl, and move, which does not contain the nature imparted by creation and transformation? Since there is no thing that does not embody this principle or contain this nature, there is no thing that creation and transformation have not brought to completion. What creation and transformation bring to completion is so abundant: what accomplishment achieved externally could surpass it? Is this not why it is called the great undertaking? 于外也紀其時夫修文德不期遠人之必至而
其至自有不容已者是宜即其事與時而紀之

益之賛即為班師振旅之舉當是時帝舜在上
亦何為哉其所以誕敷文德固自若耳想夫灼
于四方者若日照月臨燦乎文命之流行加于
百姓者若雲行雨施藹乎德教之漸被及國家
===

儀綴兆舒疾秩然其有行列蓋不復用於軍旅
之地而特在乎賔主之階則向之徂征不足事
矣然禹自班師甫及乎七旬彼苗之來格遽見
於一旦奔走京師而悔過之不遑拜稽廷陛而

史臣於聖君之修于內也，紀其事；於遠人之至于外也，紀其時。夫修文德，不期遠人之必至，而其至自有不容已者，是宜即其事與時而紀之也歟！昔大禹以苗之頑，嘗有奉辭伐罪之行；因益之賛，即為班師振旅之舉。當是時，帝舜在上，亦何為哉？其所以誕敷文德，固自若耳。想夫灼于四方者，若日照月臨，燦乎文命之流行；加于百姓者，若雲行雨施，藹乎德教之漸被。及國家之閒暇，舞干羽而雍容，屈伸俯仰，翼然其有文儀；綴兆舒疾，秩然其有行列。蓋不復用於軍旅之地，而特在乎賔主之階，則向之徂征不足事矣。然禹自班師，甫及乎七旬，彼苗之來格，遽見於一旦。奔走京師而悔過之不遑，拜稽廷陛而請罪之不暇。匪招而來之也，慕吾之文命，皆將有丕叙之圖；匪俘而獻之也，感吾之德教，相率有即工之念。則向之逆命不足言矣。然則敷文德者，舜素敷耳，非自班師而始敷；有苗格者，苗
translation_en:
Examiner Peng, Academician, comments: Skillful in trimming and shaping, without overstepping the rules.

When the sage ruler cultivated virtue within his realm, the court historian recorded his deeds; when people from afar arrived from beyond it, he recorded the time. In cultivating civil virtue, one does not expect that distant peoples must necessarily come; yet their coming has an impetus that cannot be restrained. Surely it was fitting to record both the deeds and their timing!

Formerly, because of the obstinacy of the Miao, the Great Yu undertook a campaign to proclaim their offenses and punish their crimes. Following Yi’s counsel, however, he immediately withdrew his troops and brought his army home. At that time, with Emperor Shun ruling above, what did he do? He simply continued, as before, to spread civil virtue far and wide. Imagine its brilliance throughout the four quarters, like the shining sun and the moon looking down: how splendidly his civil commands circulated! Its influence upon the common people was like moving clouds and falling rain: how abundantly his virtuous instruction gradually spread over them!

When the state was at peace, dancers bearing shields and pheasant plumes performed with dignified ease. Bending and stretching, bowing and rising, they displayed a stately ceremonial grace; in their dance positions and the slowness or speed of their movements, their ranks were orderly. These implements were no longer employed on the battlefield, but only at the steps where host and guest met. Thus the earlier punitive expedition no longer merited pursuit.

Yet scarcely seventy days after Yu withdrew his army, the Miao suddenly came and submitted. They hurried to the capital, scarcely able to repent their faults quickly enough; they bowed and knocked their heads upon the ground at the court steps, scarcely able to beg forgiveness quickly enough. They had not been summoned and brought there: admiring our civil commands, they all intended to enter into the great order. Nor had they been captured and presented as prisoners: moved by our virtuous instruction, they encouraged one another in the wish to attend to their duties. Thus their earlier defiance of commands no longer merited mention.

Accordingly, as for spreading civil virtue, Shun had always spread it; he did not begin only after the army’s withdrawal. As for the Miao’s submission, the Miao…

translation_en:
…came over of their own accord; it was not only after the dance with shields and plumes that they submitted. The historian recorded these events together, allowing us to envision the flourishing age of Shun of Youyu across a thousand years. Yet I have examined the Book of Documents: Shun had already done everything possible in dealing with the insignificant Miao people. After they had submitted on this occasion, he subsequently dispersed them northward, which shows that they were still not fully transformed. The Miao were a different people; what personal prejudice could Shun have harbored? He knew only to devote himself to spreading his civil virtue. In the end, Shun let his robes hang down, and all under Heaven governed itself; those dispersed northward no longer resisted his transforming influence. Yi’s words of praise were thus all the more fully borne out!
“Formerly, under Kings Wen and Wu, who were perceptive, discerning, and consummately sage, ministers great and small all cherished loyalty and goodness.”
Wang Zongqi

This essay alone, without wasting words, fully elucidates the idea of the Zhou dynasty’s sage rulers and worthy ministers, leaving nothing unexplained. It certainly deserves to be recorded.

title: 成化二十年會試錄
text:
文矣
考試官庶子劉批語簡而勁
考試官學士彭批辭不繁而意足
賢王之述盛世君既備其德而臣皆同乎德甚
矣君聖臣賢不易得也非盛世之為君臣者其
孰能然哉昔穆王命伯冏為太僕正而告之以
此意謂世道莫盛於我周君德莫過於文武以
言其德聰無不聞而足以達天下之隱明無不
見而足以燭天下之微曰聰曰明文武無二致
===
也齊無不敬合動靜而咸肅聖無不通隨事物
而周知曰齊曰聖文武同一揆也蓋君德之備
如此其在當時小而百僚庶采大而公卿大夫
位雖有崇卑罔不夙夜匪懈恪恭廼職而懷夫
忠以事君不忠者無有焉官雖有大小靡不精
白一心守德不回而懷夫良以事君不良者無
有焉蓋臣德之同又如此吁我周盛時明良相
逢尚有賴於近習之助矧予小子德不逮於文
武而臣未得乎忠良可不資爾伯冏以為助乎

punctuated:
文矣。
考試官庶子劉批：語簡而勁。
考試官學士彭批：辭不繁而意足。
賢王之述盛世，君既備其德，而臣皆同乎德。甚矣，君聖臣賢不易得也！非盛世之為君臣者，其孰能然哉？昔穆王命伯冏為太僕正，而告之以此，意謂世道莫盛於我周，君德莫過於文武。以言其德，聰無不聞，而足以達天下之隱；明無不見，而足以燭天下之微。曰聰曰明，文武無二致也。齊無不敬，合動靜而咸肅；聖無不通，隨事物而周知。曰齊曰聖，文武同一揆也。蓋君德之備如此。其在當時，小而百僚庶采，大而公卿大夫，位雖有崇卑，罔不夙夜匪懈，恪恭廼職，而懷夫忠以事君，不忠者無有焉；官雖有大小，靡不精白一心，守德不回，而懷夫良以事君，不良者無有焉。蓋臣德之同又如此。吁！我周盛時，明良相逢，尚有賴於近習之助，矧予小子德不逮於文武，而臣未得乎忠良，可不資爾伯冏以為助乎？
translation_en:
…writing indeed.
Examiner Liu, Junior Supervisor of Instruction, comments: “The language is concise and forceful.”
Examiner Peng, Academician, comments: “The wording is economical, yet the meaning is fully expressed.”
In a worthy king’s account of a flourishing age, the ruler possessed virtue in its completeness, and his ministers all shared in that virtue. How very difficult it is to find a sage ruler and worthy ministers! Who but the ruler and ministers of a flourishing age could achieve this? In former times, King Mu appointed Bo Jiong Grand Coachman and instructed him in these terms. His meaning was this: “No age has flourished more than that of our Zhou, and no rulers have surpassed Kings Wen and Wu in virtue. To speak of their virtue: their keen hearing missed nothing, enabling them to apprehend all that was hidden in the world; their clear sight overlooked nothing, enabling them to illuminate all that was subtle in the world. In keen hearing and clear sight, Wen and Wu were alike. In reverence, they neglected nothing, maintaining solemnity in both activity and repose; in sagely understanding, nothing eluded them, and they comprehended every affair and thing. In reverence and sagely understanding, Wen and Wu followed the same standard. Such was the completeness of their virtue as rulers.
“At that time, from the lesser officials holding the various offices to the highest dukes, ministers, and grandees, although their ranks differed in eminence, all worked tirelessly from morning to night, reverently attending to their duties and serving their rulers with loyalty in their hearts. There was none who was disloyal. Although their offices differed in importance, all kept their hearts wholly pure and single-minded, holding fast to virtue without deviation and serving their rulers with goodness in their hearts. There was none who lacked goodness. Such, too, was the shared virtue of the ministers.
“Ah! In our Zhou’s flourishing age, enlightened rulers and good ministers encountered one another, yet they still depended on the assistance of close attendants. How much more must I, the young one, whose virtue falls short of Wen and Wu’s and who has yet to obtain loyal and good ministers, rely on you, Bo Jiong, for assistance?”

translation_en:
In general, whether a ruler’s close attendants are upright or depraved determines whether his virtue is perfected. Those who occupy these positions must therefore be carefully chosen. If unsuitable men are appointed, their influence gradually permeates him morning and evening, drawing him into wickedness without his knowing it. Even worthy counselors can then do nothing about it. This is why King Mu dwelt so earnestly on this matter when issuing his charge. Should not those who possess all under Heaven also give it their attention?

Book of Odes
“The king is at Hao; how grand is his dwelling!”
By Zhou Dong.

Comment by Associate Examiner Yang, Supervising Secretary: The essay’s tenor is dignified and solemn, like an upright gentleman whose measured bearing inspires respect in those who see him. Compared with it, those who parade superficial phrases without any foundation would have to retreat far more than three marching stages!

Comment by Associate Examiner Zeng, Senior Compiler: Its portrayal of the feudal lords’ intention to bestow praise upon the king of Zhou makes one feel as though present at that time. Could anyone read it without seeing its author in a new light?

Comment by Associate Examiner Wu, Senior Compiler: The topic from “Fish and Waterweed” (Yu zao) left many candidates in the examination hall at a loss. No other essay has depicted the atmosphere of peace under the Zhou house as this one has. We therefore record it as a model for students of the Book of Odes.

Comment by Associate Examiner Li, Expositor: Among the essays interpreting the Lesser Odes (Xiao ya), this alone is stately and weighty, free of superficiality, and distinct from the other compositions.

title: 成化二十年會試錄
text:
考試官庶子劉批歸美之詞宜如此
考試官學士彭批題短能不窘
諸侯之美天子必言其尊臨乎王都而安處乎
天位也夫王都乃天下之所尊瞻而天位宜人
君之所安處也詩人以是而美天子有周盛時
氣象固如是哉昔天子燕諸侯而諸侯美天子
若曰吾王膺景命而紹大統履至尊而撫鴻圖
今果何在乎則在乎鎬京也是鎬之為京據天
下之都會當諸夏之要衝翼翼乎其整敕巍巍
===
乎其壮麗吾王之臨御於斯也居重馭輕誠足
以為萬邦之方宅中圖大誠足以建四方之極
夫王之在於鎬京一日二日萬幾宜其不遑少
暇矣然當是時重熙累洽而海宇昇平仁深澤
厚而民物康阜政務不憂於叢脞不過端冕凝
旒安居於九重以常享至治之福猶北辰不動
而眾星自拱也宵旰無事乎經營不過垂紳正
笏端拱於穆清以坐收太平之効猶岱嶽常尊
而眾山自宗也吁盛時王者氣象豈不洋溢於

今果何在乎則在乎鎬京也是鎬之為京據天

夫王之在於鎬京一日二日萬幾宜其不遑少

諸侯之美天子，必言其尊臨乎王都而安處乎天位也。夫王都乃天下之所尊瞻，而天位宜人君之所安處也。詩人以是而美天子，有周盛時氣象固如是哉！昔天子燕諸侯，而諸侯美天子，若曰：「吾王膺景命而紹大統，履至尊而撫鴻圖，今果何在乎？則在乎鎬京也。是鎬之為京，據天下之都會，當諸夏之要衝，翼翼乎其整敕，巍巍乎其壮麗。吾王之臨御於斯也，居重馭輕，誠足以為萬邦之方；宅中圖大，誠足以建四方之極。夫王之在於鎬京，一日二日萬幾，宜其不遑少暇矣。然當是時，重熙累洽而海宇昇平，仁深澤厚而民物康阜。政務不憂於叢脞，不過端冕凝旒，安居於九重，以常享至治之福，猶北辰不動而眾星自拱也。宵旰無事乎經營，不過垂紳正笏，端拱於穆清，以坐收太平之効，猶岱嶽常尊而眾山自宗也。」吁！盛時王者氣象，豈不洋溢於

Examiner Peng, Academician, comments: “Though the topic is short, the writer succeeds in avoiding constraint.”

When the feudal lords praise the Son of Heaven, they invariably speak of his presiding in majesty over the royal capital and dwelling at ease in his Heaven-bestowed position. The royal capital is what all under Heaven look up to with reverence, and the Heaven-bestowed position is where the ruler should dwell at ease. The poet praises the Son of Heaven on these grounds. Was this indeed the atmosphere of the flourishing age of Zhou!

In former times, the Son of Heaven feasted the feudal lords, and they praised him, as though saying: “Our king has received the great Mandate and succeeded to the great line of rule; he occupies the most exalted position and presides over the vast imperial domain. Where, then, is he now? He is in Haojing. As a capital, Hao occupies the meeting place of all under Heaven and commands the strategic crossroads of the various Xia states. How imposing its orderly arrangement, how lofty its magnificence! Our king reigns here, occupying the seat of central authority and thereby controlling the lesser regions: truly he can serve as the model for the myriad states. Dwelling at the center and planning great undertakings, truly he can establish the guiding standard for the four quarters.

“While the king resides in Haojing, each day brings countless matters requiring his attention; one would expect him to have not a moment’s leisure. Yet at this time, successive ages of prosperity and accumulated good government have brought peace throughout the realm; profound benevolence and abundant beneficence have brought well-being and plenty to the people and all living things. There is no fear that affairs of government will become tangled in petty details. He need only wear his ceremonial crown upright, its pendants hanging still, and dwell at ease within the ninefold palace, continually enjoying the blessings of consummate government—just as the Pole Star remains motionless while the other stars naturally pay it homage. He has no need to labor over affairs from before dawn until late at night. He need only let his great sash hang down, hold his tablet upright, and sit with folded hands in the solemn purity of his court, reaping the fruits of perfect peace without stirring—just as Mount Dai remains ever exalted while the other mountains naturally acknowledge its supremacy.”

Examiner Peng, Academician, comments: “This captures Duke Wu’s intent in admonishing himself.”
In admonishing himself, the worthy lord wished to fulfill all the duties appropriate to every place within his reach. For leaving nothing unconsidered in his deliberations and nothing unattended in his preparations were all matters of governing the state. Could the worthy lord have sought to fulfill his proper duties in each place without understanding the essentials of government? In former times, Duke Wu of Wei composed a poem and had others recite it to admonish him. His meaning was that places within and without differed, and their affairs differed accordingly. Could one who governed a state fail to deliberate thoroughly and make orderly preparations as each affair required? Thus, morning and night, he maintained regular times for retiring and rising; within his residence, sprinkling and sweeping were invariably attended to. These were minor, routine affairs within the court. Who would not suppose that, because they concerned places so close at hand, they might perhaps be neglected? Yet how could they know that those above set the example for those below? His thorough attention to retiring and rising, sprinkling and sweeping was intended to give the common people an example to observe and follow in activity and rest, so that they too would know that retiring and rising must never be left to indulgence; and to give them a model for daily life, so that they too would know that sprinkling and sweeping must never be treated carelessly. Nor was this all. Chariots and horses were the means of overcoming enemies, so he put them in order and brought them to the utmost strength and vigor. Bows, arrows, and weapons of war were the means of guarding against trouble, so he likewise put them in order and brought them to the finest condition. These were preparations against the non-Chinese frontier regions—great affairs involving unforeseen changes. Who would not suppose that, because they concerned places so far away, they might perhaps be passed over? Yet how could they know that danger lies hidden in security? translation_en:
…act recklessly [?]? When hostilities arise, knowing that we are on our guard, would they not submit in fear and flee? Ah! Let deliberation be thorough within, neglecting nothing because it is near; let preparations be put in order without, overlooking nothing because it is distant. All this amounts to nothing more than a single reverent and cautious heart. When that heart manifests itself in affairs, all affairs are well handled: how could the state fail to be well governed? Profound indeed is the intention to admonish oneself!

Further examination of this poem shows that it comprises ten stanzas. This stanza begins, “August Heaven does not approve,” and then follows with these words. This is truly because, in seeking good government, what a ruler must bear in mind is Heaven’s intention. Mindful of Heaven’s intention, he will know reverence and fear; following this with reforms to government admits of no delay. The sage emperors and enlightened kings of old brought the world to great peace by following this way. How much more, then, should Duke Wu, as ruler of Wei, have done so! Yet Duke Wu was wise and sagely: it was fitting that he knew to exert himself in this. Should not later rulers of states and domains, reciting the admonitory poem “Yi” (Admonition), exert themselves still more in this regard?

《春秋》譏伯主勤兵以畧遠，而美伯主仗義以服強。此見齊桓之北伐山戎，不若南征荆楚之為得也。在昔北戎病燕，職貢不至。齊桓内無因國之助，外無諸侯之從，躬率師旅以伐山戎，非但使職貢之通，抑欲使土地之闢。自常情言之，桓公此舉克盡方伯之職矣。《春秋》何以譏之乎？聖人以為蕞爾北戎，非門庭之寇，宜以德綏者也。桓也文德不修，大義不舉，徒越千里之險，力爭不毛之地，勞中國而事外夷，舍近政而務遠畧。借曰戎狄是膺，而所以膺戎者非其道矣。故特貶而稱人，以為好武功、不修文德者之戒。若夫荆楚不道，駕禍諸姬，齊桓内連八國之師，外結江黃之援，執言伐楚，按兵于陘。楚人震恐，而屈完寔來；召陵退師，而盟禮遂定。自常情言之，桓
translation_en:
…there is one as accomplished as this: it is like a celestial steed coursing through the sky, naturally standing apart from the herd. It has therefore been recorded to serve as a model for students of the Classics.
Examiner Liu, Mentor, comments: In discussing Duke Huan of Qi’s successes and failures, the language is concise and exacting.
Examiner Peng, Academician, comments: Neither the achievements nor the faults of a hegemon obscure the other. This composition grasps that point.
The Spring and Autumn Annals censures a hegemon who exhausts his armies in conquering distant lands, but praises a hegemon who upholds righteousness to subdue the powerful. This shows that Duke Huan of Qi’s northern campaign against the Shanrong was less justified than his southern expedition against Jingchu. Formerly, the northern Rong afflicted Yan, preventing its prescribed tribute from arriving. Duke Huan of Qi had neither the assistance of supporting states [?] within nor the participation of the feudal lords without. He personally led his armies against the Shanrong, intending not only to reopen the tribute routes but also to expand territory. Judged by ordinary sentiments, Duke Huan fully discharged his duties as a regional overlord in this undertaking. Why, then, does the Spring and Autumn Annals censure him? The Sage considered the insignificant northern Rong no enemy at the gates: they should have been pacified through virtue. Yet Huan cultivated no civil virtue and upheld no great principle of righteousness. He merely crossed a thousand li of perilous terrain to fight for barren land, exhausting the Central States in dealing with the outer barbarians and neglecting government close at hand to pursue distant conquests. Even granting that he was ‘striking against the Rong and Di,’ the means by which he struck against the Rong were improper. Thus the text deliberately lowers his standing by calling him simply a ‘man,’ as a warning to those who prize military achievements but do not cultivate civil virtue.
As for Jingchu, it flouted the Way and brought calamity upon the states of the Ji lineage. Duke Huan of Qi united the armies of eight states within his alliance and secured support from Jiang and Huang outside it. He advanced a rightful cause for attacking Chu and halted his troops at Xing. The people of Chu were terrified, and Qu Wan did indeed come. The army withdrew to Shaoling, and the covenant rites were duly settled. Judged by ordinary sentiments, Huan…

title: 成化二十年會試錄
text:
公此舉似無撻伐之威矣春秋何以美之乎聖
人以為蠢爾荆蠻大邦為仇非可以力勝者也
桓也不遺一矢不血一刃但責彼王貢胡為不共
問彼王舟胡為不復以律用師而不輕以義致
楚而不暴雖曰擅興征伐而所以伐楚者有其
道矣故特詳序其績以為修文德柔服遠人者
之勸孟子謂春秋無義戰彼善於此則有之說
者以為召陵之師是已然則伐楚豈獨善於伐
戎哉聖人譏彼而美此其致意於桓公者深矣
===
大抵五伯桓公為盛以其有安攘之功故也然
楚方受盟志已驕溢陳濤塗一謀不協其身見
執其國見伐見侵而怒猶未息量小而器不宏
如此視彼成湯勝夏撫有萬方而慄慄危懼者
度量相越何其遠哉此君子所以貴王而賤伯
公會晋侯及吳子于黄池哀公十三年
倪綱

公會晉侯及吳子于黃池〔襄公十三年〕
倪綱

punctuated:
公此舉似無撻伐之威矣，《春秋》何以美之乎？聖人以為蠢爾荆蠻，大邦為仇，非可以力勝者也。桓也不遺一矢，不血一刃，但責彼王貢胡為不共，問彼王舟胡為不復。以律用師而不輕，以義致楚而不暴，雖曰擅興征伐，而所以伐楚者有其道矣。故特詳序其績，以為修文德、柔服遠人者之勸。孟子謂：「春秋無義戰，彼善於此則有之。」說者以為召陵之師是已。然則伐楚豈獨善於伐戎哉？聖人譏彼而美此，其致意於桓公者深矣。
大抵五伯，桓公為盛，以其有安攘之功故也。然楚方受盟，志已驕溢。陳濤塗一謀不協，其身見執，其國見伐、見侵，而怒猶未息。量小而器不宏如此，視彼成湯勝夏、撫有萬方而慄慄危懼者，度量相越何其遠哉！此君子所以貴王而賤伯。
「公會晋侯及吳子于黄池。」哀公十三年。

translation_en:
…this undertaking of Duke Huan seems to have displayed none of the might of punitive conquest. Why, then, does the Spring and Autumn Annals praise it? The Sage considered that the unruly southern peoples of Jing, enemies of the great states, could not be overcome by force. Huan discharged not a single arrow and bloodied not a single blade. He merely demanded to know why they had failed to supply tribute to the king, and asked why the king’s boat had never returned. He employed his army according to established rules, without recklessness, and brought Chu to submission through righteousness, without violence. Although he undertook a punitive expedition on his own authority, his manner of campaigning against Chu accorded with the proper Way. Thus the Annals gives a particularly detailed account of his achievement, to encourage those who cultivate civil virtue and win the submission of distant peoples through gentleness. Mencius said: “In the Spring and Autumn period there were no righteous wars, though some were better than others.” Commentators take the expedition to Shaoling as just such a case. Was the campaign against Chu, then, merely better than the campaign against the Rong? In censuring the latter and praising the former, the Sage’s intentions concerning Duke Huan were profound indeed.
Of the Five Hegemons, Duke Huan was, on the whole, the most eminent, because he secured peace within and repelled threats from without. Yet scarcely had Chu accepted the covenant when his ambitions overflowed with arrogance. When a single proposal by Chen Taotu displeased him, he had the man seized and his state attacked and invaded; still his anger did not subside. Such were his narrow tolerance and limited capacity. Compare him with Cheng Tang, who conquered Xia and took possession of the myriad regions, yet trembled with apprehension: how far apart they were in breadth of mind! This is why the gentleman esteems true kingship and holds hegemony in low regard.
“The duke met with the Marquis of Jin and the Viscount of Wu at Huangchi.” Thirteenth year of Duke Ai.
Ni Gang
Comment by Associate Examiner Zhao, Secretary: This essay has expressive force and decisive judgment. It stands far above those that merely copy the commentarial tradition without being able to integrate and comprehend it…

夷夏大防春秋所謹得不於黃池之會而寓意
===
哉何則春秋之末世伯者晉爭伯者吳晉自召
陵以来日漸衰微吳自柏舉之後勢傾上國一
旦即黃池之地講會盟之禮二國偕臨我公在
列而吳也僭稱王號侈然以自尊敢爭晉長偃
然而先歃聖人修經至此以為晉吳之會兩伯
並興先吳則拂經而失序列書則泯實而傳疑
故特以晉及吳書及者以此及彼之辭兩相敵
之義也而兩伯之實可見矣夫晉伯雖衰主盟
猶在列國諸侯未之或先也吳以何人而敢先

同考試官修撰林批：「黃池書法，類能講之，但條達精詳，鮮有髙此篇者。」

考試官庶子劉批：「春秋以天理裁世事，於此作見之。」

考試官學士彭批：「內夏外夷之旨，說得明白。」

春秋著內外之兩伯，必紀其常而正其名也。盖夷夏大防，春秋所謹，得不於黃池之會而寓意哉？何則？春秋之末，世伯者晉，爭伯者吳。晉自召陵以来，日漸衰微；吳自柏舉之後，勢傾上國。一旦即黃池之地，講會盟之禮，二國偕臨，我公在列。而吳也，僭稱王號，侈然以自尊，敢爭晉長，偃然而先歃。聖人修經至此，以為晉吳之會，兩伯並興，先吳則拂經而失序，列書則泯實而傳疑。故特以晉及吳書。及者，以此及彼之辭，兩相敵之義也，而兩伯之實可見矣。夫晉伯雖衰，主盟猶在，列國諸侯未之或先也。吳以何人而敢先
translation_en:
… Indeed. It is recorded here as a model.

Associate Examiner Lin, Senior Compiler, comments: “Most can explain the wording used for Huangchi, but few essays surpass this one in orderly exposition, precision, and detail.”

Examiner Liu, Vice Supervisor of Instruction, comments: “The Spring and Autumn Annals judges worldly affairs by Heaven’s principles. This essay brings that out.”

Examiner Peng, Academician, comments: “The principle of treating the Chinese states as insiders and the non-Chinese as outsiders is explained clearly.”

When the Spring and Autumn Annals records the two hegemons, one within and one outside the Chinese realm, it necessarily records the enduring norms and rectifies their designations. The great boundary between the non-Chinese and the Chinese is something the Annals carefully safeguards. How, then, could it fail to convey its meaning in recording the meeting at Huangchi? Why is this so? Toward the end of the Spring and Autumn period, Jin held the established hegemony, while Wu contested it. Since the meeting at Shaoling, Jin had grown weaker by the day; after the battle of Boju, Wu’s power overshadowed the states of the central realm. When they came to Huangchi to perform the ceremonies of meeting and covenant, both states were present, and our duke stood among the participants. Yet Wu usurped the royal title, exalted itself extravagantly, dared to contest Jin’s precedence, and arrogantly took the covenant blood first.

When the Sage reached this event in compiling the Classic, he considered that the meeting of Jin and Wu marked the simultaneous emergence of two hegemons. To place Wu first would violate the enduring norm and upset the proper order; to list them without distinction would obscure the facts and transmit uncertainty. He therefore specifically wrote “Jin and Wu.” The word “and” connects this party with that party and signifies that the two stand as rivals. Thus the reality of the two hegemonies becomes apparent. Although Jin’s hegemony had declined, its authority to preside over covenants remained: none of the lords of the various states had taken precedence over it. Who was Wu to dare take precedence …

title: 成化二十年會試錄
text:
晉軟邪苟不後之則內外之常典紊矣故吳雖
主會而特先晉者內中國而外四夷所以紀其
常也况天無二日民無二王普天率土莫非周
之臣也吳以何人而敢僭王號邪苟不正之則
上下之名分泯矣故吳雖僭王特以子書四夷
雖大皆稱子所以正其名也觀此可見聖人順
天地之經著盟會之實惡夷狄之强而抑其横
所以訓後世治中國御四夷之道不亦深切而
著明哉抑考之吳嘗破越又嘗破楚又嘗勝齊
===
至是遂長晉矣自謂莫之敵也抑豈知爭盟未
退而於越已入其國都嗣子之俘姑蘇之焚大
舟之徙吳亦不能免哉曾子曰出乎爾者反乎
爾信夫
禮記
大學之敎也時敎必有正業退息必有居
學不學操縵不能安弦不學博依不能安
詩不學雜服不能安禮不興其藝不能樂
學故君子之於學也藏焉修焉息焉遊焉

退而於越已入其國都嗣子之俘姑蘇之焚大

爾信夫

學故君子之於學也藏焉修焉息焉游焉
punctuated:
晉軟邪？苟不後之，則內外之常典紊矣。故吳雖主會，而特先晉者，內中國而外四夷，所以紀其常也。况天無二日，民無二王，普天率土，莫非周之臣也。吳以何人而敢僭王號邪？苟不正之，則上下之名分泯矣。故吳雖僭王，特以子書，四夷雖大皆稱子，所以正其名也。觀此，可見聖人順天地之經，著盟會之實，惡夷狄之强而抑其横，所以訓後世治中國、御四夷之道，不亦深切而著明哉！抑考之，吳嘗破越，又嘗破楚，又嘗勝齊，至是遂長晉矣，自謂莫之敵也。抑豈知爭盟未退，而於越已入其國都，嗣子之俘、姑蘇之焚、大舟之徙，吳亦不能免哉！曾子曰：「出乎爾者，反乎爾。」信夫！
禮記
大學之敎也，時敎必有正業，退息必有居學。不學操縵，不能安弦；不學博依，不能安詩；不學雜服，不能安禮；不興其藝，不能樂學。故君子之於學也，藏焉，修焉，息焉，遊焉。
translation_en:
…take precedence over Jin [?]? If Wu were not placed after it, the established distinction between those within and those outside would be thrown into disorder. Thus, although Wu presided over the gathering, Jin was deliberately placed first: this treated the Central States as within and the barbarians of the four quarters as outside, thereby recording the enduring norm. Moreover, Heaven has no two suns, and the people have no two kings. Throughout all beneath Heaven, to the boundaries of the earth, none were other than subjects of Zhou. Who was the ruler of Wu to dare usurp the title of king? If this were not corrected, the distinctions of status between superior and subordinate would be effaced. Thus, although Wu usurped the royal title, its ruler was expressly recorded as a viscount. However great the barbarian states of the four quarters might be, their rulers were all styled viscounts: this served to rectify their titles.
From this we can see that the Sage followed the constant principles of Heaven and Earth and made clear the actual circumstances of covenant meetings. He abhorred the strength of the barbarians and restrained their overbearing conduct. Was not the way in which he thereby instructed later generations in governing the Central States and controlling the barbarians of the four quarters profound, pertinent, and manifestly clear? On further examination, Wu had defeated Yue, defeated Chu, and overcome Qi; now it finally took precedence over Jin, imagining that none could rival it. Yet how could it have known that, before it withdrew from its contest for precedence at the covenant meeting, Yuyue had already entered its capital? Wu could not escape the capture of its heir, the burning of Gusu, or the removal to Dazhou [?]. Master Zeng said: “What goes forth from you returns to you.” How true!
Record of Rites (Liji)
In the teaching of the Great Learning, instruction at the prescribed times must have its regular coursework, and retirement for rest must have its private study. Without learning to practise on unadorned strings, one cannot become at ease with stringed music; without learning broadly through analogies, one cannot become at ease with the Odes; without learning miscellaneous duties, one cannot become at ease with ritual. Unless one cultivates an interest in these arts, one cannot delight in learning. Thus, in learning, the gentleman stores it in his heart, cultivates it, rests in it, and takes his recreation in it.

Teaching provides a complete method for timely diligence; learning prizes the effort of timely diligence. Such was the Great Learning of antiquity. Learning becomes effortless and reaches completion because there is no time at which one is not diligent. The teacher’s methods are comprehensive, and the learner’s efforts are sustained and thorough: is this not why accomplishment comes readily? Moreover, if the gentleman wishes to transform the people and perfect their customs, he must proceed through the Great Learning. Thus, when a king establishes a state and rules its people, he must give priority to teaching and learning. But what, precisely, was instruction in the ancient college like?

title: 成化二十年會試錄
text:
何如哉凡學之道貴乎能安而底于成未至于
安在乎為之而不可厭彼教必有絃也習絃於
學而不操弄於退息必不能使手安於絃矣教
必有詩也講詩於學而不博物於退息必不能
使心安於詩矣教必有禮也而禮必有服焉不
觀雜服於退息而但學行禮於學校則亦不能
安於禮矣夫絃詩禮之學即所謂正業也操縵
博依雜服之藝即所謂居學也既退息而不興
三者之藝又安得謂之好學哉是故君子之於
===
學也藏焉修焉之時必正業之是樂則所習者
專而志不分息焉遊焉之際必居學之是興則
所養者純而藝愈熟古之人所以敬遜時敏者
如此然則其成材之易也宜哉大抵一張一弛
固文武之道而一曝十寒未有能生之物此所
以時教退息之有節而正業居學之無間也又
不特此耳自家有塾而至國有學則養之有其
序自視離經辨志而至强立不反則考之以其
漸先王教學之法至矣安親樂信之益近悅遠

punctuated: 何如哉？凡學之道，貴乎能安而底于成。未至于安，在乎為之而不可厭。彼教必有絃也，習絃於學而不操弄於退息，必不能使手安於絃矣。教必有詩也，講詩於學而不博物於退息，必不能使心安於詩矣。教必有禮也，而禮必有服焉。不觀雜服於退息，而但學行禮於學校，則亦不能安於禮矣。夫絃詩禮之學，即所謂正業也；操縵博依雜服之藝，即所謂居學也。既退息而不興三者之藝，又安得謂之好學哉？是故君子之於學也，藏焉修焉之時，必正業之是樂，則所習者專而志不分；息焉遊焉之際，必居學之是興，則所養者純而藝愈熟。古之人所以敬遜時敏者如此，然則其成材之易也宜哉！大抵一張一弛，固文武之道，而一曝十寒，未有能生之物。此所以時教退息之有節，而正業居學之無間也。又不特此耳，自家有塾而至國有學，則養之有其序；自視離經辨志而至强立不反，則考之以其漸。先王教學之法至矣！安親樂信之益，近悅遠
translation_en:
…what should they be like? In all learning, what matters is to become at ease with it and thereby attain accomplishment. Before reaching such ease, one must work at it without growing weary. Instruction necessarily includes stringed music. If one practices it at school but does not play during periods of rest, one cannot make one’s hands at ease with the strings. Instruction necessarily includes the Odes. If one studies the Odes at school but does not broaden one’s knowledge of things during periods of rest, one cannot make one’s mind at ease with the Odes. Instruction necessarily includes ritual, and ritual necessarily involves dress. If one does not examine the various kinds of dress during periods of rest, but merely learns to perform ceremonies at school, one likewise cannot become at ease with ritual. The study of stringed music, the Odes, and ritual constitutes what is called the regular curriculum; the arts of practicing miscellaneous tunes, drawing widely on analogies, and studying various kinds of dress constitute what is called study outside formal lessons. If, upon withdrawing to rest, one does not take up these three arts, how can one be called a lover of learning?
Thus, in learning, when the gentleman applies himself inwardly and cultivates his studies, he must delight in the regular curriculum: what he practices will then be focused, and his purpose undivided. During rest and recreation, he must take up study outside formal lessons: what he cultivates will then be pure, and his skills increasingly practiced. This is how the people of antiquity were reverent, compliant, and diligent at all times. It is fitting, then, that they should so readily have become accomplished! In general, alternately drawing the bow taut and relaxing it was indeed the Way of Kings Wen and Wu; yet nothing can grow if exposed to warmth for one day and cold for ten. This is why scheduled instruction and periods of rest are properly regulated, while the regular curriculum and study outside formal lessons continue without interruption.
Nor is this all. From the teaching hall serving local households to the school in the capital, students were nurtured in an ordered sequence. From examining their ability to analyze the classics and discern their aspirations to assessing their ability to stand firm without turning back, they were examined by gradual stages. The former kings’ methods of teaching and learning were perfected indeed! The benefits of honoring one’s parents and delighting in trustworthy companions, and of pleasing those nearby and those far away…

懷之效豈偶然哉
和故百物皆化序故羣物皆别
黃金
同考試官給事中劉批樂記一題講和
序處多欠明白惟此作發揮透徹是用錄出
同考試官右諭德謝批昭晰者無疑優
游者有餘此作其庶幾乎場中得之亦難矣

考試官學士彭批典實可嘉
===
惟造化著動靜之妙故物類遂生成之天盖陽
動而和陰靜而序此造化自然之妙也然則物
類之生成豈不各由之而遂哉記者論禮樂之
所本而及此意謂天地之道動而為陽靜而為
陰以其陽之動言之則春生夏長合同而為和
吾見下降上躋一至和之磅礴相摩相蕩一至
和之充周天地和而百物有不化乎由是若飛
若潜莫不相育於昡合之中若動若植罔不相
養於絪縕之內物類雖萬不齊同一化醇之天

惟造化著動靜之妙，故物類遂生成之天。盖陽動而和，陰靜而序，此造化自然之妙也。然則物類之生成，豈不各由之而遂哉？記者論禮樂之所本而及此，意謂天地之道，動而為陽，靜而為陰。以其陽之動言之，則春生夏長，合同而為和。吾見下降上躋，一至和之磅礴；相摩相蕩，一至和之充周。天地和，而百物有不化乎？由是若飛若潜，莫不相育於昡合之中；若動若植，罔不相養於絪縕之內。物類雖萬不齊，同一化醇之天
translation_en:
…the effect of winning the allegiance of those afar—could it be merely accidental?

“Through harmony, all things undergo transformation; through order, all things are differentiated.”
By Huang Jin.

Associate Examiner Liu, Supervising Secretary, comments: “On this topic from the Record of Music, most answers lack clarity in their treatment of harmony and order. This composition alone develops the meaning thoroughly; therefore it has been selected for inclusion.”
Associate Examiner Xie, Right Admonisher, comments: “What is lucid leaves no doubt; what unfolds at ease has ample scope. This composition comes close to that standard! Such a piece is difficult to find even among examination submissions.”
Examiner Liu, Secretariat Supervisor, comments: “It is indeed correct to argue that ritual and music have their foundation in the creative transformations of nature.”
Examiner Peng, Academician, comments: “Its grounding in the classics and its substance are commendable.”

It is because the creative transformations of nature manifest the subtle workings of movement and stillness that the various kinds of things fulfill their natural course of generation and development. Yang moves and produces harmony; yin is still and produces order: these are the spontaneous, subtle workings of creation. How, then, could the generation and development of each kind of thing fail to proceed through these workings to fulfillment? The author of the Record reaches this point in discussing the foundation of ritual and music. His meaning is that, in the Way of Heaven and Earth, movement constitutes yang and stillness constitutes yin. Speaking of the movement of yang, things are born in spring and grow in summer; their union and convergence constitute harmony. I see descending and ascending forces, all one vast expanse of perfect harmony; their mutual contact and agitation, all one pervasive fullness of perfect harmony. When Heaven and Earth are harmonious, can any of the myriad things fail to undergo transformation? Thus, whether flying or submerged, all nurture one another amid this mysterious conjunction [?]; whether moving creatures or rooted plants, all sustain one another within the intermingling of vital forces. Though the kinds of things are myriad and diverse, they share a single natural process of transformation into full maturity…

矣。所謂「品物咸亨」者，此也。以其陰之靜言之，則秋斂冬藏，分辨而為序。吾見溫厚轉為嚴凝，而秩然之分以見；和同返為閉塞，而截然之等以明。天地序，而羣物有不別乎？由是或高或下，連而不相及也；或大或小，動而不相害也。物類雖萬不一，各一散殊之天矣。所謂「各正性命」者，此也。夫和而化，則同者不容以獨異；序而別，則異者不可以强同。聖人制禮作樂，寧不於是而效法乎？抑論之，一動一靜，固天地之分，而動者又未嘗不本於靜也。然則一和一序，固禮樂之情，而樂之作，亦安可不先序以禮乎？周子曰：「萬物各得其理而後和，故禮先而樂後。」其深知禮樂之本矣。

translation_en:
…This is what is meant by “the myriad things all flourish.” Speaking of yin’s stillness, autumn gathers in and winter stores away: differentiation produces order. I see warmth and mildness turn to severity and cold, revealing orderly distinctions; harmonious unity returns to closure and obstruction, making sharply defined gradations clear. When Heaven and Earth are ordered, could the myriad things fail to be differentiated? Thus, whether high or low, they are connected without encroaching upon one another; whether large or small, they move without harming one another. Though the kinds of things are myriad and diverse, each has its own distinct endowment from Heaven. This is what is meant by “each correctly realizes its nature and allotted destiny.” When harmony brings transformation, things that are alike cannot stand apart in solitary difference; when order brings differentiation, things that differ cannot be forcibly made alike. In instituting ritual and creating music, how could the sages fail to take this as their model?
To consider it further, activity and stillness are indeed distinct aspects of Heaven and Earth, yet activity is never without its foundation in stillness. Harmony and order are indeed the essential qualities of music and ritual; how, then, could music be created without first establishing order through ritual? Master Zhou said: “Only after the myriad things each attain their proper principle is there harmony. Thus ritual comes first and music afterward.” He understood profoundly the foundation of ritual and music.

Associate Examiner Zeng, Senior Compiler, comments: Among those writing in this examination, not one is truly precise and pertinent. In seeking a work that restrains ornament in favor of substance and deeply grasps the purport of the Comprehensive Writings (Tongshu), I have found only this essay. It should be recorded as a model for future students.

Associate Examiner Wu, Senior Compiler, comments: Its language is concise and antique, yet its meaning is not obscure. It is an outstanding work among the discourses in this examination.

Associate Examiner Li, Expositor, comments: Writers of discourses commonly regard striking grandeur and rich ornament as marks of excellence, yet these amount to mere words. Examiner Liu, Vice Supervisor of Instruction, comments: In composing a discourse, what matters is tracing things from their source through their ramifications and offering elucidation, rather than merely multiplying words. title: 成化二十年會試錄
text:
文以顯文其不朽之器載斯道而行於無
窮者乎如其道之不載則虛器耳不適於
用其何取於文哉嗟夫道在天地間不可
一日焉無者其原出於天其綱在於仁義
禮智其端見於惻隱羞惡辭讓是非其事
形於彝倫其功至於治國平天下其效可
以位天地而育萬物然行道者世不常有
也不託之文則道或晦焉塞焉不傳焉君
子不得已而有文也夫豈好為無益之辭
===
哉然世之作者多矣其不傳者奚啻什百
譬之車焉以載物也而輪轅必飾欲其人
之愛而用也君子者篤於道德而文辭必
其兼美美則人自愛之愛則傳之千萬世
而不朽賢者因是得以學焉君子為教於
後世有益於人遠矣是猶車飾焉而人用
也然世之人不能皆賢也不賢者雖父兄
臨之師保勉之耳提而面命諄諄焉誨也
猶不肯一從寧肯從事於簡冊之陳言乎

臨之師保勉之耳提而面命諄諄焉誨也
猶不肯一從寧肯從事於簡冊之陳言乎
punctuated:
文以顯。文，其不朽之器，載斯道而行於無窮者乎？如其道之不載，則虛器耳，不適於用，其何取於文哉？嗟夫！道在天地間，不可一日焉無者。其原出於天，其綱在於仁義禮智，其端見於惻隱羞惡辭讓是非，其事形於彝倫，其功至於治國平天下，其效可以位天地而育萬物。然行道者，世不常有也。不託之文，則道或晦焉，塞焉，不傳焉。君子不得已而有文也，夫豈好為無益之辭哉？

然世之作者多矣，其不傳者奚啻什百？譬之車焉，以載物也，而輪轅必飾，欲其人之愛而用也。君子者篤於道德，而文辭必其兼美。美則人自愛之，愛則傳之千萬世而不朽。賢者因是得以學焉，君子為教於後世，有益於人遠矣。是猶車飾焉而人用也。然世之人不能皆賢也。不賢者，雖父兄臨之，師保勉之，耳提而面命，諄諄焉誨也，猶不肯一從，寧肯從事於簡冊之陳言乎？
translation_en:
…writing to make it manifest. Is writing not an imperishable vessel that carries this Way onward without end? If it does not carry the Way, it is merely an empty vessel, unfit for use. What value, then, would writing have? Alas! The Way cannot be absent from between Heaven and Earth for even a single day. Its source is Heaven; its guiding principles are benevolence, righteousness, ritual propriety, and wisdom. Its beginnings appear in compassion, shame and aversion to wrongdoing, deference and yielding, and the discernment of right and wrong. Its practical expression lies in the enduring human relationships; its accomplishments extend to governing the state and bringing peace to all under Heaven. Its efficacy can set Heaven and Earth in their proper places and nurture the myriad things. Yet those who put the Way into practice are not always present in the world. Unless it is entrusted to writing, the Way may become obscured, obstructed, and cease to be transmitted. The gentleman thus produces writing out of necessity. How could he merely delight in composing useless words?

Yet there have been many writers in the world. How could those whose works have not been transmitted number merely in the tens or hundreds? Consider a carriage: its purpose is to carry things, yet its wheels and shafts must be ornamented so that people will cherish and use it. The gentleman is devoted to the Way and virtue, and his language must also possess beauty. If it is beautiful, people will naturally cherish it; if they cherish it, they will transmit it through thousands upon thousands of generations, and it will endure imperishably. Through it, worthy people are able to learn. By providing instruction for later generations, the gentleman benefits people far into the future. This is like ornamenting a carriage so that people will use it. Yet not everyone in the world can be worthy. As for the unworthy, even when fathers and elder brothers oversee them and teachers and guardians exhort them, pulling them by the ear and instructing them face to face, teaching them earnestly and patiently, they still refuse to comply even once. How, then, would they be willing to apply themselves to the old sayings recorded in books?

title: 成化二十年會試錄
text:
言雖至文而人弗從文亦末如之何也已
車已飾而人弗用亦虛飾焉矧其不務道
德而徒勞心思弊精神馳騁於文辭以為
能文雖至工亦不過藝焉而已文不載道
無益於世教猶不載物之車也徒美其飾竟
何為哉在昔三代以上如易以道陰陽書
以道政事詩以道性情春秋以道名分禮
樂以道序和孔孟從而贊述焉而道賴以
傳其文之醇後世莫及然其所以醇而不
===
可及者豈無所自哉而世或莫之識也三
代以下道學不明其摛章繪句文非不工
而於道判然雖無作可已所幸天不喪文
道未墜地以至有宋諸君子如周程張朱
者出其文足以羽翼乎六經孔孟而道賴
以益明矣逮我
聖朝又從而表章之於是斯道昭如日星嗚呼
文明之盛何幸於
今日見之

言雖至文，而人弗從，文亦末如之何也已。車已飾，而人弗用，亦虛飾焉。矧其不務道德，而徒勞心思、弊精神，馳騁於文辭，以為能文，雖至工，亦不過藝焉而已。文不載道，無益於世教，猶不載物之車也。徒美其飾，竟何為哉？
在昔三代以上，如《易》以道陰陽，《書》以道政事，《詩》以道性情，《春秋》以道名分，禮樂以道序和，孔孟從而贊述焉，而道賴以傳。其文之醇，後世莫及。然其所以醇而不可及者，豈無所自哉？而世或莫之識也。三代以下，道學不明，其摛章繪句，文非不工，而於道判然，雖無作可已。所幸天不喪文，道未墜地，以至有宋諸君子，如周程張朱者出，其文足以羽翼乎六經、孔孟，而道賴以益明矣。逮我聖朝，又從而表章之，於是斯道昭如日星。嗚呼！文明之盛，何幸於今日見之！
translation_en:
…Even if the words attain the utmost literary beauty, if people will not follow them, literature can do nothing about it. If a carriage has been ornamented but people will not use it, its ornamentation is likewise in vain. How much more so when someone neglects the Way and virtue, merely taxing his thoughts and exhausting his spirit, ranging freely through literary expression and considering himself an accomplished writer! However consummate his skill, it amounts to no more than an art. Writing that does not carry the Way and does nothing to advance moral teaching in the world is like a carriage that carries no goods. What, ultimately, is the use of merely beautifying its ornamentation?
In antiquity, during the Three Dynasties and earlier, the Changes expounded yin and yang; the Documents, affairs of government; the Odes, human nature and feelings; the Spring and Autumn Annals, distinctions of name and status; and rites and music, order and harmony. Kongzi and Mengzi followed, elucidating and transmitting these teachings, and through them the Way was handed down. Later ages could not match the purity of their writing. Yet could this purity, which others could not equal, have been without a source? People sometimes fail to recognize it. After the Three Dynasties, learning concerning the Way became obscure. Writers fashioned ornate compositions and embellished sentences; their writing was certainly skillful, yet it stood wholly apart from the Way. Such works might just as well have remained unwritten. Fortunately, Heaven did not extinguish this cultural inheritance, and the Way did not fall into oblivion. In time, the gentlemen of the Song arose—Zhou, Cheng, Zhang, and Zhu. Their writings were sufficient to support the Six Classics and the teachings of Kongzi and Mengzi, and through them the Way became still clearer. Then our sagely dynasty further honored and promoted these teachings, so that this Way shines as brightly as the sun and stars. Ah! How fortunate we are to witness such a flourishing of civilization today!

translation_en: …such are those who do not write merely for writing’s sake. If one writes merely for its own sake, one’s craftsmanship may indeed be accomplished and one’s language beautiful. To compose it oneself and admire it oneself is well enough; but to wish everyone to admire it is to wish for what cannot be attained. To admire it oneself and transmit it oneself is well enough; but to wish everyone to transmit it is to wish for what cannot be attained. If it is neither admired nor transmitted, it serves no purpose in the world. Its presence adds nothing, and its absence leaves nothing lacking. What use, then, is writing? Surely there must be writing of the highest order, which none but a sage can produce. Ah! Writing conveys the Way: is this not writing of the highest order? Yet the Way is difficult to understand; how, then, could writing be easy to produce? The Book of Changes says: “Observe the patterns of Heaven to discern the changes of the seasons; observe human patterns to transform and perfect all under Heaven.” Such, indeed, was the ancient sages’ contemplation of patterns. Yet once the seasonal changes had been discerned and all under Heaven transformed and perfected, could the sages remain indifferent to later generations and simply forget them? In looking down and looking up, they brought together the Ways of Heaven and humanity to consolidate the substance of their writing, and brought together the patterns of Heaven and humanity to refine its artistry. They gave expression to what flowed from this abundance, and thus their writing conveyed the Way. Hence the writing of the Book of Changes conveys the Way of yin and yang; that of the Book of Documents conveys the Way of government; that of the Book of Odes conveys the Way of human nature and feelings; the writings on rites and music convey the Way of equilibrium and harmony; and that of the Spring and Autumn Annals conveys the Way of rewards and punishments. These are the most conspicuous examples of their writing. This is writing of the highest order, produced for more than writing’s sake. Had the sages in their own time forgotten later generations, and the Six…

title: 成化二十年會試錄
text:
經不作道不幾於缺乎蓋易不作則陰陽
之道缺書不作則政事之道缺詩不作則
性情之道缺禮樂不作則中和之道缺春
秋不作則賞罰之道缺作則完不作則缺
吾是以知聖人為後世計固有不得已者
使其得已而不已則是有意於文矣有意
於文是專於藝者之所為惡得為載道之
文哉嗟夫後世之文皆得已而不已者也
有意於文者也故文愈繁而道愈窒愛之
===
者愈多然而知道者不愛也傳之者愈遠
然而知道者不傳也甚矣後世之文之叛
道也春秋戰國而降其人可數歷數百年
而漢始得董仲舒之三策然不能無陰陽
縱閉之說又數百年而唐始得韓愈之原
道然不能無博愛謂仁之說此其道雖載
而不能盡載者非其文之晦而不能彰也
非其文之弱而不能勝也惟其見於道者
之未純故其發於文者自雜也雖然是豈

經不作，道不幾於缺乎？蓋《易》不作，則陰陽之道缺；《書》不作，則政事之道缺；《詩》不作，則性情之道缺；禮樂不作，則中和之道缺；《春秋》不作，則賞罰之道缺。作則完，不作則缺。吾是以知聖人為後世計，固有不得已者。使其得已而不已，則是有意於文矣。有意於文，是專於藝者之所為，惡得為載道之文哉！

嗟夫！後世之文，皆得已而不已者也，有意於文者也。故文愈繁而道愈窒，愛之者愈多，然而知道者不愛也；傳之者愈遠，然而知道者不傳也。甚矣，後世之文之叛道也！春秋戰國而降，其人可數。歷數百年，而漢始得董仲舒之三策，然不能無陰陽縱閉之說；又數百年，而唐始得韓愈之《原道》，然不能無博愛謂仁之說。此其道雖載而不能盡載者，非其文之晦而不能彰也，非其文之弱而不能勝也，惟其見於道者之未純，故其發於文者自雜也。雖然，是豈
translation_en:
…Classics had not been composed, would not the Way have been left incomplete? For if the Book of Changes had not been composed, the Way of yin and yang would have been incomplete; without the Book of Documents, the Way of government would have been incomplete; without the Book of Odes, the Way of human nature and feelings would have been incomplete; without the works on ritual and music, the Way of equilibrium and harmony would have been incomplete; without the Spring and Autumn Annals, the Way of rewards and punishments would have been incomplete. With these works, it is complete; without them, it is incomplete. From this I know that, in providing for later generations, the sages truly acted out of necessity. Had they been able to refrain yet not refrained, they would have been deliberately pursuing literary accomplishment. Such a pursuit is the work of those who devote themselves exclusively to literary craft. How could it produce writing that conveys the Way?

Alas! The writings of later ages are all works whose authors could have refrained from writing but did not: they deliberately pursued literary accomplishment. Thus, the more abundant the writings, the more obstructed the Way. Those who admire them grow ever more numerous, yet those who understand the Way do not admire them; those who transmit them carry them ever farther, yet those who understand the Way do not transmit them. How grievously the writings of later ages have departed from the Way! From the Spring and Autumn and Warring States periods onward, the men who conveyed it in writing can be counted. Several hundred years passed before the Han produced Dong Zhongshu’s Three Policy Essays, yet even these were not free of theories concerning yin and yang and “release and closure” [?]. Several hundred more years passed before the Tang produced Han Yu’s Inquiry into the Way (Yuan Dao), yet even this was not free of the assertion that universal love is called benevolence. That these works convey the Way but cannot convey it fully is not because their writing is too obscure to make it manifest, nor because their writing is too weak to bear it. It is simply that their authors’ understanding of the Way was not yet pure, so its expression in their writing was naturally mixed with extraneous elements. Even so, could it be that…
