translation_en:
…could there ultimately have been no such person? Indeed, several hundred more years passed before a great Confucian emerged in the Song: Master Zhou. The forty chapters of his Comprehensive Writings (Tongshu) arose from his tacit apprehension of the substance of the Way; this was certainly not something attained through study. The statement that “writing serves to convey the Way” also describes his own work. After Master Zhou took the lead with the Comprehensive Writings, Master Cheng followed with his Commentary on the Changes, and Master Zhang followed with Correcting Youthful Ignorance and the Eastern and Western Inscriptions. With Master Zhu, the abundance of such writings reached its height. Were these gentlemen not also examples of those whose writing attained the highest excellence and was not produced in vain?
Writing, then, may be compared to a cart, and the Way to its load. A cart must carry something to be useful; an empty cart will not do. Writing must convey the Way to be useful; empty writing will not do. Adorn its wheels and shafts, and everyone will admire it; if there are then those who put it to use, that is no fault of mine [?]. Refine the wording, and everyone will admire it; if there are then those who transmit it, that is no fault of mine [?]. As for those whom fathers and elder brothers oversee and teachers and guardians encourage, “those who do not act in vain are unworthy” [?]; what blame can I bear? Those who do not know to devote themselves to the Way and virtue, but strive instead to display their ability through literary expression, are shallow people. What can I expect of them? This, too, is Master Zhou’s meaning.

I humbly submit: under Your Majesty’s sagely rule, governing without exertion, the transforming influence of civilization spreads throughout the realm. The ancestral house of the Confucian tradition has cause for celebration, and its temple walls shine with added moral radiance. All scholars rejoice together; we descendants are especially fortunate. Reverently engraving this kindness upon our hearts and gratefully receiving Your virtue, we respectfully bow our heads to the ground and lift our voices in praise. Looking upward to Your sunlike countenance, we feel keen trembling within, as though treading on ice.

We humbly reflect that Your Majesty the Emperor maintains a mind profound and sincere, and firmly upholds Heaven’s mandate in solemn purity. Succeeding to the throne and preserving its achievements, You continue the great legacy of the one Founding Ancestor and the four Ancestral Emperors. Esteeming the worthy and seeking good government, You extend the grand designs of the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors. Your virtue is renewed daily, and renewed yet again; though Your Way has attained perfection, You pursue it as though perfection remained unattained. You drive out the lingering adherents of heterodox teachings and uphold the authoritative tradition of orthodox learning. You consider how the achievement of editing and transmitting the Six Classics serves, for ten thousand generations, as the foundation of the cardinal bonds and constant virtues…

translation_en:
…a rule. Though the spirit of Niqiu—Confucius—has long since departed, it still abides in the sanctuary at Queli. Temples to him have spread throughout the realm, yet his sacrificial worship is especially splendid in this one town. Recently, overflowing rainwater and floods caused the temple buildings to collapse. Although dwelling comfortably in fine halls was not his original aspiration when he practiced the Way, displaying reverence and giving his spirit repose are indeed the grand observances through which later generations honor their teacher. The prescribed numbers of sacrificial vessels and ranks of ritual dancers had already been increased to enhance the ceremonies; now an imperial edict has again ordered the rebuilding of the rear hall, main hall, gates, and covered galleries. The expenses are met from funds accumulated in the government treasury, and oversight of the work is entrusted specifically to the regional authorities. The timber is excellent, gathered from the trees of Xinfu and Culai; those attending to the work are reverent, with men in scholars’ broad-sleeved robes and ritual caps hastening to serve. The images and their adornments are solemn and dignified, and the old objects are preserved. Although the work was begun without urging haste, the hall was soon completed and afforded perfect repose. The clans of the state gather here [?]: what need is there to await Zhang Lao’s blessing? The rites of Zhou are all preserved here: they may yet draw another visit of inspection like that of Ji Zha.
Your servant’s learning falls short of his family’s inherited tradition, and his abilities are limited by Heaven. Undeservedly ranked among the highest dukes, I am ashamed to lack even the abilities of a lower serviceman. For successive years I have unworthily received glory and honor; today I have once more encountered your abundant favor. How could your servant dare fail to observe the rites of [four illegible characters], thereby following what remains of his father’s instruction; to strive to be filial and strive to be loyal, [three illegible characters] the weight of this felicitous favor [?]. Humbly I wish that Heaven may be clear and Earth tranquil, and that the fortunes of letters and of the age may flourish together; that, like rivers flowing and the sun ascending, Your Majesty’s sacred longevity and the longevity of the state may endure together. Your servant cannot contain his feelings as he gazes …

title: 成化二十年會試錄
text:
朝典則超邁前古其大者有十二其可以示天下萬世而不刊夷
有定天下之大功有治天下之大法蓋功
之定天下者在於一時而法之治天下者
垂於萬世考之往古驗之方今有以見我
朝
太祖高皇帝之盛德大業過於前代帝王遠矣
哉請因明問而條陳之唐虞以来治化莫
盛於三代三代相繼制度莫備於成周然

===

會同之有儀冠婚喪祭之有禮車服器用
之有差貢賦征徭之有等斟酌損益鉅細

而開賢良方正之科禁蘇張申韓之學正

朝典則超邁前古，其大者有十二，其可以示天下萬世而不刊夷。

有定天下之大功，有治天下之大法。蓋功之定天下者在於一時，而法之治天下者垂於萬世。考之往古，驗之方今，有以見我朝太祖高皇帝之盛德大業過於前代帝王遠矣哉！請因明問而條陳之。唐虞以来，治化莫盛於三代；三代相繼，制度莫備於成周。然武王受命於倦勤之日，而不及為；周公輔相於孺子之朝，而始有作。自今觀之，朝覲會同之有儀，冠婚喪祭之有禮，車服器用之有差，貢賦征徭之有等，斟酌損益，鉅細畢舉，此有周之制所以為善也。厥後嬴秦失鹿，漢有天下。高帝規摹非不弘遠也，然而開賢良方正之科，禁蘇張申韓之學，正朔之改，經籍之表章，不能不待於文武之世者，非以混一之初未暇為邪？隋政不綱，唐混六合。高祖謀猷非不周密也，然而律
translation_en:
…our dynasty’s institutions and regulations far surpass those of antiquity. Their principal features number twelve, and they can serve as an immutable standard for all under Heaven through the myriad generations [?].

There are great achievements that bring all under Heaven to order, and great laws by which all under Heaven is governed. Achievements that bring the realm to order belong to a single age, whereas laws that govern it are handed down through myriad generations. Examining antiquity and testing it against the present, we can see how far the abundant virtue and great accomplishments of our dynasty’s Taizu, the Gao Emperor, surpass those of the emperors and kings of earlier ages! Allow me to respond to your illuminating question by setting these matters out in order.

Since the ages of Tang Yao and Yu Shun, government and moral transformation have never flourished more than under the Three Dynasties. Among those successive dynasties, institutions were never more complete than under Zhou. Yet King Wu received the mandate when already weary of his labors and did not have time to establish them; only when the Duke of Zhou assisted the young ruler did their creation begin. Viewed from the present, there were prescribed ceremonies for court audiences and assemblies, rites for capping, marriage, mourning, and sacrifice, distinctions in carriages, dress, implements, and utensils, and graded obligations for tribute, taxation, levies, and labor service. Reductions and additions were carefully weighed, and matters great and small were all addressed. This is what made Zhou’s institutions good.

Later, the Ying house of Qin lost its hold on the realm, and Han possessed all under Heaven. Emperor Gao’s plans were certainly broad and far-reaching. Yet the establishment of the category for recruiting the Worthy and Good, Upright and Correct; the prohibition of the teachings of Su Qin, Zhang Yi, Shen Buhai, and Han Fei; the alteration of the calendar and the beginning of the year; and the honoring and promotion of the classical texts all had to await the reigns of Emperors Wen and Wu. Was this not because, in the first days of unification, there had been no time to undertake them?

Sui’s government lost its guiding order, and Tang united the realm. Gaozu’s plans were certainly comprehensive and meticulous. Yet the statutes…

text:
令之定雅樂之成曆書之考服制之更不
能不待於太宗之世者非締造之始未暇
及邪至於五代訖運宋祖隆興開寶初政
非不善也然崇天之曆尚待於天聖之時
學校之興猶在於慶曆之日非以方平僭
偽享國未久而不克詳且盡歟然則具
聖德而操制作之權享

punctuated: 令之定，雅樂之成，曆書之考，服制之更，不能不待於太宗之世者，非締造之始未暇及邪？至於五代訖運，宋祖隆興，開寶初政非不善也，然崇天之曆尚待於天聖之時，學校之興猶在於慶曆之日，非以方平僭偽，享國未久，而不克詳且盡歟？然則具聖德而操制作之權，享聖壽而兼創守之責，自有周以来，未有若我高皇帝者也。逐窮虜於萬里，取天下於腥羶之餘，頒正朔於八荒，復綱常於淪斁之後，規畫詳明，足以建諸天地而不悖；典則精密，足以質諸鬼神而無疑。請舉其大者言之：大祀南郊，而每歲一行，不簡不瀆，此事天之謹也；嶽鎮海瀆，而去其封號，不褻不誣，此事神之正也。嚴宮闈之禁，而朝政不干，齊家之法何其周！隆宗藩之封，而民事不干，睦族之法何其至！郡縣設學校，而惟教以經術，養士之法遠追
translation_en:
…the settling of ordinances, the establishment of ritual music, the examination of calendrical writings, and the revision of regulations for dress all had to await the reign of Taizong: was this not because, at the dynasty’s founding, there had been no leisure to attend to them? When the allotted fortunes of the Five Dynasties came to an end and the founding emperor of the Song rose to power, the early government of the Kaibao era was certainly good. Yet the Chongtian calendar still had to await the Tiansheng era, and the flourishing of schools came only in the Qingli era. Was this not because he had only just subdued the illegitimate regimes and had ruled for too short a time to make his arrangements detailed and complete? Thus, in possessing sagely virtue and wielding the authority to establish institutions, enjoying a sage’s longevity and bearing responsibility both for founding and for preserving the dynasty, none since the Zhou has equaled our Emperor Gao.

He drove the desperate barbarians ten thousand li away and took possession of All under Heaven after its defilement by their rank and mutton-scented rule. He promulgated the imperial calendar throughout the eight wildernesses and restored the cardinal bonds and constant virtues after their collapse and corruption. His plans were detailed and clear, fit to be established between Heaven and Earth without contradiction; his institutions and standards were exact and meticulous, fit to be submitted to the spirits for judgment without doubt. Allow me to discuss their principal features. The great sacrifice at the southern suburban altar was performed once each year, neither neglectfully nor with irreverent repetition: such was his care in serving Heaven. He removed the enfeoffed titles of the sacred peaks, guardian mountains, seas, and great rivers, avoiding both profanation and false attribution: such was his correctness in serving the spirits. He made the restrictions governing the inner palace strict, so that its members did not interfere in court government: how comprehensive were his methods of regulating the family! He bestowed exalted fiefs upon the imperial princes, yet they did not interfere in the people’s affairs: how consummate were his methods of maintaining harmony among his kinsmen! He established schools in prefectures and counties, teaching only classical learning: his methods of nurturing scholars reached far back to emulate…

text:
乎成周科舉用經術而不雜以詞賦取士
之法誠過於唐宋語紀元之法則一定不
更視漢以來數改年號者何繁邪語設官
之法則六卿分職視秦以來專任宰相者
何偏邪四方水旱而優卹之恩必下此養
民之法也四夷僻遠而征討之兵不加此
待夷狄之法也婚姻之禮非但革胡元之
汙而屬戚不混又有歷代以來所未備者
儀文之懿非但革胡元之陋而上下有章
===
又具兩漢以來所未有者
律詳五刑而輕重適中
令舉六綱而大小有序
大誥有三編而申明五常之條秩如也
資世有通訓而戒飭四民之章煥如也以至
孝慈有錄禮儀有式教民有榜彰善癉惡有
書于以垂世教而淑人心于以正神人而
厚風俗長治久安其策端在此矣由此觀
之則知我

乎成周。科舉用經術而不雜以詞賦，取士之法誠過於唐宋。語紀元之法，則一定不更，視漢以來數改年號者，何繁邪？語設官之法，則六卿分職，視秦以來專任宰相者，何偏邪？四方水旱，而優卹之恩必下，此養民之法也。四夷僻遠，而征討之兵不加，此待夷狄之法也。婚姻之禮，非但革胡元之汙，而屬戚不混，又有歷代以來所未備者。儀文之懿，非但革胡元之陋，而上下有章，又具兩漢以來所未有者。
律詳五刑，而輕重適中；令舉六綱，而大小有序。《大誥》有三編，而申明五常之條秩如也；資世有通訓，而戒飭四民之章煥如也。以至孝慈有錄，禮儀有式，教民有榜，彰善癉惡有書，于以垂世教而淑人心，于以正神人而厚風俗。長治久安，其策端在此矣。由此觀之，則知我

…to the Zhou at its height. The civil-service examinations employ classical learning, unmixed with verse and rhapsodies: this method of selecting officials truly surpasses that of the Tang and Song. As for the system of reckoning reign eras, once established, an era name is not changed. How needlessly frequent, by comparison, were the changes of era name since the Han! As for the organization of offices, the Six Ministers divide their responsibilities. How unbalanced, by comparison, was exclusive reliance on chief ministers since the Qin! When floods or droughts strike any part of the realm, generous relief is invariably bestowed: this is the method of nurturing the people. Although the barbarians of the four quarters inhabit remote regions, punitive armies are not sent against them: this is the method of dealing with foreign peoples. Marriage rites have not merely eliminated the defilement of the barbarian Yuan; they also prevent confusion in kinship relationships and include provisions lacking throughout previous dynasties. The excellence of ceremonial forms has not merely eliminated the crudeness of the barbarian Yuan; it also provides clear rules for superiors and inferiors, incorporating things absent even since the two Han dynasties.
The statutes detail the five punishments, striking a proper balance between severity and leniency; the ordinances set out six principal divisions, ordering matters both great and small. The Grand Pronouncements (Da Gao) comprise three compilations, whose provisions expounding the Five Constant Virtues are systematically arranged. For the guidance of the world there are Comprehensive Admonitions (Tong Xun), whose articles admonishing the four occupational groups are luminously clear. There is also a Record of Filial Piety and Parental Kindness, prescribed forms for ritual and ceremony, placards for instructing the people, and a book for commending good and condemning evil. Through these, moral instruction is handed down and people’s hearts are improved; through these, the relations of spirits and humans are set right and customs are made wholesome. translation_en:
…our sagely founder received Heaven’s mandate as did King Wu, yet the excellence of his institutions did not have to await a Duke of Zhou. He founded his dynasty as did the founders of the Han, Tang, and Song, yet the completeness of his statutes and institutions required no further labor from succeeding generations. Thus his achievements surpassed those of a hundred kings, and his governance exceeded that of the Three Dynasties, bequeathing to his sagely sons and divine grandsons an excellent plan for countless generations. The Commentary says: “Shun established a model for all under Heaven that could be transmitted to later generations.” This describes our sagely founder. It is also said: “Without conscious knowledge or understanding, they followed the Lord’s pattern.” How fortunate are the people of this age! Respectfully submitted in reply.

title: 成化二十年會試錄
text:
平正是足以觀其所養矣
考試官庶子劉批條答古今風俗敎化之原如
指諸掌且詞氣充暢必佳士也
考試官學士彭批此策言敷敎化必由於公薦舉
明義理可謂知所本矣
薦舉之途難公公則僥倖者無所容義理
之學難明明則奔競者當自息蓋義理之
學微由功利詞章之說勝薦舉之途塞由
請託貨賂之私行以是而欲風俗正敎化
===
行亦憂憂乎其難矣昔唐虞三代聖君賢
相共成光明正大之業薦舉之途公而野
無遺賢如舜舉於側微說舉於版築是已
義理之學明而士有定守如伊尹安於耕
太公安於漁是已自成周選舉之制壞而
僥倖之門開自戰國遊說之風興而奔競
之途啓以後世用人言之如漢武帝疇咨
海內舉其俊茂宣帝講論六藝招選茂異
畏義好賢能用忠謀則有如唐之太宗憲

考試官學士彭批：此策言敷敎化必由於公薦舉、明義理，可謂知所本矣。
薦舉之途難公，公則僥倖者無所容；義理之學難明，明則奔競者當自息。蓋義理之學微，由功利詞章之說勝；薦舉之途塞，由請託貨賂之私行。以是而欲風俗正、敎化行，亦憂憂乎其難矣！昔唐虞三代，聖君賢相共成光明正大之業，薦舉之途公而野無遺賢，如舜舉於側微、說舉於版築是已；義理之學明而士有定守，如伊尹安於耕、太公安於漁是已。自成周選舉之制壞，而僥倖之門開；自戰國遊說之風興，而奔競之途啓。以後世用人言之，如漢武帝疇咨海內，舉其俊茂；宣帝講論六藝，招選茂異；畏義好賢，能用忠謀，則有如唐之太宗、憲
translation_en:
…is balanced and sound; this suffices to reveal the cultivation he has attained.
Examiner Liu, Secretariat Supervisor, comments: His answers address, point by point, the origins of customs and moral transformation in ancient and recent times, making them as clear as something pointed out in one’s palm. Moreover, his language is vigorous and fluent. He must be an excellent scholar.
Examiner Peng, Academician, comments: This policy essay argues that extending moral instruction must proceed through impartial recommendations for office and the clarification of moral principles. He may be said to understand the foundation.
It is difficult to make the channels of recommendation impartial; when they are impartial, those seeking advancement through undeserved good fortune have no place. It is difficult to make the study of moral principles clear; when it is clear, those scrambling for advancement should desist of their own accord. The study of moral principles has declined because doctrines of profit and advantage and literary composition have prevailed; the channels of recommendation have become blocked because private solicitation and bribery are practiced. Under these circumstances, to wish for customs to be rectified and moral instruction to take effect is indeed distressingly difficult [?]!
Formerly, in the ages of Tang and Yu and the Three Dynasties, sage rulers and worthy ministers together accomplished enlightened and upright undertakings. Recommendations were impartial, and no worthy men remained overlooked outside office: Shun’s elevation from humble obscurity and Yue’s from rammed-earth construction exemplify this. The study of moral principles was clear, and scholars held steadfast convictions: Yi Yin’s contentment with farming and Taigong’s contentment with fishing exemplify this. Once the selection system of the established Zhou order broke down, the door to undeserved advancement opened; once the practice of itinerant persuasion arose in the Warring States period, the paths of competitive office-seeking opened.
As for the employment of men in later ages, Emperor Wu of the Han sought counsel throughout the realm and raised up its outstanding talents; Emperor Xuan discussed the Six Arts and recruited men of exceptional ability. Among those who revered righteousness, cherished worthy men, and could act upon loyal counsel were the Tang emperors Taizong and Xian…

title: 成化二十年會試錄
text:
宗不輕任人責成輔相則有如宋之太祖
仁宗之數君者固能用賢矣然廣利以嬖
寵封侯寬饒以公清獲罪魏徵不能終其
寵夷簡得以乆其權蓋徒欣慕其名未盡其
實所謂薦舉之公者吾未敢必以為然也
以後世士風言之如汲黯之獨揖衛青嚴光
不拜諫議韓維安於靜退不就廷試尹焞
耻議正人不復應舉以見王公為自鬻者
陳師道也以勤職事為求知者吕舜從也
===
之數人者固能守巳以正矣然漢雖有齊魯諸
儒之傳授宋雖有濂洛大儒之倡和而當
時尚通者多守義者少所謂義理之明者
吾亦未敢必以為然也夫薦舉不公義理
不明而欲望風俗之正教化之行以追唐
虞三代之盛夫豈能哉方今
聖天子夙夜孜孜留心政理其用人也銓曹之
黜陟風紀之臧否薦舉之途公矣而僥倖
之徒猶存者無乃請託貨賂之私有未盡

陳師道也以勤職事為求知者呂舜從也
===

黜陟風紀之臧否薦舉之途公矣而僥倖
之徒猶存者無乃請託貨賂之私有未盡
punctuated:
宗。不輕任人，責成輔相，則有如宋之太祖、仁宗之數君者，固能用賢矣。然廣利以嬖寵封侯，寬饒以公清獲罪，魏徵不能終其寵，夷簡得以乆其權，蓋徒欣慕其名，未盡其實。所謂薦舉之公者，吾未敢必以為然也。
以後世士風言之，如汲黯之獨揖衛青，嚴光不拜諫議，韓維安於靜退，不就廷試，尹焞耻議正人，不復應舉，以見王公為自鬻者，陳師道也；以勤職事為求知者，吕舜從也。之數人者，固能守巳以正矣。然漢雖有齊魯諸儒之傳授，宋雖有濂洛大儒之倡和，而當時尚通者多，守義者少。所謂義理之明者，吾亦未敢必以為然也。
夫薦舉不公，義理不明，而欲望風俗之正、教化之行，以追唐虞三代之盛，夫豈能哉？
方今聖天子夙夜孜孜，留心政理。其用人也，銓曹之黜陟，風紀之臧否，薦舉之途公矣。而僥倖之徒猶存者，無乃請託貨賂之私有未盡
translation_en:
…Xianzong. As for not appointing men lightly and holding chief ministers responsible for results, there were such rulers as Taizu and Renzong of the Song. These rulers certainly knew how to employ worthy men. Yet Guangli was enfeoffed as a marquis through personal favor, while Kuanrao incurred punishment despite his impartiality and integrity; Wei Zheng could not retain imperial favor to the end, while Yijian was able to hold power for a long time. They evidently admired the reputation of employing worthy men without fully realizing its substance. I therefore dare not affirm that their recommendations were truly impartial.
As for the conduct of scholars in later ages, Ji An alone greeted Wei Qing with a bow rather than prostrating himself; Yan Guang declined appointment as Remonstrator; Han Wei was content with quiet retirement and did not present himself for the court examination; and Yin Tun, ashamed to criticize upright men, never again took the examinations. It was Chen Shidao who regarded visiting princes and high ministers as selling himself, and Lü Shuncong who regarded diligently performing official duties as seeking recognition [?]. These men certainly maintained their integrity through upright conduct. Yet although the Han had the teachings transmitted by the Confucian scholars of Qi and Lu, and the Song had the great Confucian scholars of Lian and Luo advocating and responding to one another’s teachings, many in those times valued accommodation, while few upheld righteousness. I therefore also dare not affirm that moral principles were truly understood.
If recommendations are partial and moral principles are not understood, how could one hope to rectify customs and bring moral transformation into effect, thereby matching the flourishing ages of Yao and Shun and the Three Dynasties?
Today, our sagely Son of Heaven works diligently from dawn to night, devoting his attention to good government. In his employment of men, the personnel authorities determine demotions and promotions, and the censorial authorities assess merit and fault: the channels of recommendation are impartial. Yet men seeking advancement through undeserved favor still remain. Could this be because the private abuses of solicitation and bribery have not been fully…

title: 成化二十年會試錄
text:
革乎其造士也學校之講明科目之程試
義理之學明矣而奔競之風未息者無乃
入耳出口之學有未盡革乎茲欲使
朝廷之上無倖位司進退者誠得如毛玠如
張綱則勸懲當其實而薦舉之途益公士
大夫之間有節義典教化者誠得如胡瑗
如朱熹則作新有其方而義理之學益明
如是而風俗有不正教化有不行而天下
有不治吾未之信也雖然執事於此又曰
===
抑别有其故歟蓋有隱而不發之意也愚
聞之人君一身賢才之去就關焉四方之從
違繫焉故子夏曰舜有天下選於衆舉皐
陶不仁者遠矣湯有天下選於衆舉伊尹
不仁者遠矣則息僥倖止奔競蓋自有機
焉傳曰得其本萬事理孟子曰一正君而
國定其謂是歟區區迂疎之見如此不識
執事以為何如
第三問
alt_text:
單乎其造士也學校之講明科目之程試
義理之學明矣而奔競之風未息者無乃
入耳出口之學有未盡革乎茲欲使
朝廷之上無倖位司進退者誠得如毛玠如
張綱則勸懲當其實而薦舉之途益公士
大夫之間有節義與教化者誠得如胡瑗
如朱熹則作新有其方而義理之學益明
如是而風俗有不正教化有不行而天下
有不治吾未之信也雖然執事於此又曰
===
抑別有其故歟蓋有隱而不發之意也愚
聞之人君一身賢才之去就關焉四方之從
違繫焉故子夏曰舜有天下選於衆舉皐
陶不仁者遠矣湯有天下選於衆舉伊尹
不仁者遠矣則息僥倖止奔競蓋自有機
焉傳曰得其本萬事理孟子曰一正君而
國定其謂是歟區區迂疎之見如此不識
執事以為何如
第三問
punctuated:
革乎？其造士也，學校之講明，科目之程試，義理之學明矣，而奔競之風未息者，無乃入耳出口之學有未盡革乎？茲欲使朝廷之上無倖位，司進退者誠得如毛玠、如張綱，則勸懲當其實，而薦舉之途益公；士大夫之間有節義，典教化者誠得如胡瑗、如朱熹，則作新有其方，而義理之學益明。如是而風俗有不正，教化有不行，而天下有不治，吾未之信也。雖然，執事於此又曰：「抑别有其故歟？」蓋有隱而不發之意也。愚聞之，人君一身，賢才之去就關焉，四方之從違繫焉。故子夏曰：「舜有天下，選於衆，舉皐陶，不仁者遠矣。湯有天下，選於衆，舉伊尹，不仁者遠矣。」則息僥倖、止奔競，蓋自有機焉。傳曰：「得其本，萬事理。」孟子曰：「一正君而國定。」其謂是歟？區區迂疎之見如此，不識執事以為何如？

第三問
translation_en:
…have not yet been eradicated? As for the cultivation of scholars, through instruction and elucidation in the schools and assessment in the examinations, the learning of moral principle has been made clear. Yet the practice of scrambling for advancement has not ceased. Might this be because learning that merely enters the ears and issues from the mouth has not yet been entirely eliminated? If we now wish to ensure that no one at court holds office through undeserved good fortune, and if those responsible for promotion and dismissal are truly men like Mao Jie and Zhang Gang, then rewards and punishments will accord with actual merit and fault, and the avenues of recommendation will become still more impartial. If we wish integrity and righteousness to prevail among scholar-officials, and if those charged with moral instruction are truly men like Hu Yuan and Zhu Xi, then there will be proper methods for inspiring renewal, and the learning of moral principle will become still clearer. With things thus arranged, I cannot believe that customs would remain unrectified, moral instruction fail to take effect, or the realm remain ill-governed.

Nevertheless, you ask here once more: “Or is there some other cause?” Evidently there is an implication you have left unspoken. I have heard that whether worthy and talented men withdraw or enter service depends upon the ruler himself, and that whether the people throughout the realm obey or resist hinges upon him. Thus Zixia said: “When Shun possessed the realm, he selected from among the multitude and raised Gao Yao to office, and those without benevolence withdrew. When Tang possessed the realm, he selected from among the multitude and raised Yi Yin to office, and those without benevolence withdrew.” Thus there is indeed a crucial means of ending the pursuit of undeserved advancement and stopping the scramble for office. The commentary says: “Grasp the root, and all affairs will be ordered.” Mencius says: “Once the ruler is rectified, the state is settled.” Is this not what these sayings mean? Such are my humble, impractical, and ill-informed views. I do not know what you think of them.

Third Question

title: 成化二十年會試錄
text:
同考試官郎中陳批辨析精詳探見二書
之奧是可與言理矣
同考試官編修劉批鋪叙斷制如親見諸
賢辯論而一寫之佳製也參之五策通達時務而辭
氣錞然固此理學之擴充歟
考試官庶子劉批二書之疑剖析明白非素
有定見者不能
考試官學士彭批論宋儒得失了無凝滯
其深於理者歟
===
立言固難而知言亦不易立言非得醇儒
則其言不足以盡義理之奧言立矣非得
醇儒而知之則其言之或是或非亦孰從
而定之哉知此則可以復明問之言矣夫
所謂醇儒者儒而有得乎聖人之道者也
自孔孟絕學之後歷秦而漢而唐或擇焉
而不精或語焉而不詳儒之醇者鮮矣至
于有宋周程張朱四子者出得聖人之道

立言固難，而知言亦不易。立言非得醇儒，則其言不足以盡義理之奧。言立矣，非得醇儒而知之，則其言之或是或非，亦孰從而定之哉？知此，則可以復明問之言矣。夫所謂醇儒者，儒而有得乎聖人之道者也。自孔孟絕學之後，歷秦而漢而唐，或擇焉而不精，或語焉而不詳，儒之醇者鮮矣。至于有宋，周程張朱四子者出，得聖人之道
translation_en:
Comment by Associate Examiner Chen, Director: “The distinctions are precise and the analysis thorough, probing the profound meaning of the two writings. Here indeed is someone with whom one can discuss principle.”

Comment by Associate Examiner Liu, Hanlin Compiler: “The exposition and judgments read as though the author had personally witnessed the worthies debating and set it all down—a fine composition. Considered alongside his five policy essays, it shows a thorough understanding of current affairs and a harmonious tone [?]. Surely this is an extension of his learning of principle!”

Comment by Examiner Liu, Secretariat Supervisor: “The points of doubt in the two writings are analyzed clearly. No one could accomplish this without well-established convictions.”

Comment by Examiner Peng, Academician: “His discussion of the strengths and shortcomings of the Song Confucians is entirely free of hesitation or obstruction. Surely he has a profound understanding of principle!”

Establishing teachings is certainly difficult, but understanding them is no easy matter either. Unless the person establishing teachings is a Confucian scholar of pure learning, his words cannot fully express the profundities of moral principle. Once those teachings have been established, unless a Confucian scholar of pure learning understands them, on whose authority can their truth or error be determined? Understanding this, we can respond to your discerning question. What is called a Confucian scholar of pure learning is a scholar who has attained an understanding of the Way of the sages. After the transmission of learning from Kongzi and Mengzi was broken, through the Qin, Han, and Tang dynasties, some selected teachings without sufficient discrimination, while others expounded them without sufficient detail. Confucian scholars of pure learning were few indeed. When the Song dynasty came, the four masters Zhou, Cheng, Zhang, and Zhu emerged and attained the Way of the sages …

title: 成化二十年會試錄
text:
於遺經而相與傳之始無愧乎醇儒焉周
子嘗作太極圖探無聲無臭之妙以為萬
化萬物之根蓋其言之醇者也而象山陸
氏乃詆其為老氏之宗旨以無極二字同
於老氏之言耳故朱子累以書辯之其意
以為周子所謂無極者言無形而有理而
其實則造化之樞紐品彙之根柢未嘗為
真無也豈可與老氏之徒虛無之言相並
乎朱子辯之雖甚切而陸氏竟不能從焉

punctuated:

張子嘗作《西銘》，推理一分殊之旨，以明事親事天之道，亦其言之醇者也。而龜山楊氏乃疑其同墨氏之兼愛，以民胞物與數言近於墨氏之說耳。故程子特以書曉之，其意以為張子所謂民胞物與者，言人物之稟同出乾坤，而其實則人物之生、血脉之屬，未嘗不分殊也。豈可與墨氏之流無分之愛相比乎？程子曉之既甚明，而楊氏即釋然不惑焉。夫道者，所以立言之實也。
translation_en:
…from the surviving classics and together transmitted it; only then were there scholars fully worthy of being called Confucians of pure learning. Master Zhou once composed the Diagram of the Supreme Ultimate (Taiji tu), exploring the subtlety of that which has neither sound nor smell and taking it as the root of all transformations and all things. This was indeed an expression of his pure learning. Yet Lu Xiangshan disparaged it as embodying Laozi’s fundamental teaching, merely because the two characters wuji, “without ultimate,” were also found in Laozi’s words. Master Zhu therefore repeatedly defended it in letters. His meaning was that what Master Zhou called wuji referred to having no form yet possessing principle; in its reality, it was the pivot of creation and transformation and the root of all kinds of beings, never sheer nothingness. How could it be placed alongside the talk of emptiness and nothingness of Laozi’s followers? Although Master Zhu argued the point with great earnestness, Lu ultimately could not accept it.

Master Zhang once composed the Western Inscription (Xi ming), elaborating the purport of “principle is one, but its particular manifestations are differentiated,” to illuminate the Way of serving one’s parents and serving Heaven. This too was an expression of pure learning. Yet Yang Guishan suspected that it was the same as Mozi’s inclusive love, merely because the few words “the people are my siblings, and things are my companions” seemed close to Mozi’s teaching. Master Cheng therefore wrote expressly to explain it to him. His meaning was that Master Zhang’s statement, “the people are my siblings, and things are my companions,” referred to the endowments of human beings and other things alike originating in Qian and Kun—Heaven and Earth. In actuality, however, the coming into being of humans and things and the ties of blood kinship had never lacked particular distinctions. How could this be compared with the indiscriminate love of Mozi’s followers? Master Cheng’s explanation was so clear that Yang immediately understood and was no longer perplexed. Now, the Way is the substantive foundation upon which statements are established.

title: 成化二十年會試錄
text:
醇乎道則醇乎言矣周程張朱四子皆醇
乎聖人之道者也其言之見於著述者雖
天下萬世之人皆仰而則之豈獨當時
哉楊氏始雖有疑而終則釋然其有得於
程子之訓亦多矣至於陸氏兄弟先儒嘗
論其為禪學本非有得乎聖人之道者其
不能領悟周朱二子之言也不亦宜乎愚
生晚進末學雖未窺斯道之奧而竊聞儒
先之訓矣膚淺之見願因明問而質焉

第四問
儲巏
同考試官給事中仰批考究詳而處置當
終篇感慨有餘其儒而通者
同考試官修撰曾批師井田之意匡處今時
之宜獨優衆作古人云識時務者為俊傑然則春闈
俊傑非子其誰
同考試官修撰吳批井地之策撫舊典斟酌
之以著今之可行不迂不略蓋有志於用世者也录之

As for the Lu brothers, earlier Confucian scholars once judged their learning to be Chan Buddhist learning: fundamentally, they had not grasped the Way of the sages. title: 成化二十年會試錄
text:
本之固寧不有賴於是歟請言其槩夫井
田之制始於商而成於周有阡陌以定其
經界有溝澮以時其畜洩古公疆理於岐
周曾孫疆理於原隰皆是事也江漢以北
平衍之地田皆井畫而無廢地民皆授田
而無惰農先王養民之大政固莫有過於
此者秦人始廢井田而先王之法壞矣然
而力於耕桑地無遺利頭會箕斂賦無遺
法而用事之臣各効其能如鄭國鑿渠於
===
秦而畆收一鍾李氷開渠於蜀而沃野千
里矧井田阡陌雖開而甽澮距川之法猶
有存者此其所以益富強也漢興雖因秦
舊然今年免田租惟恐傷農明年勸農桑
惟欲務本而用事之臣爭言水利如兒寬
鑿六輔渠而高仰以饒白公鑿池陽區而
京師用給况當時水衡有都尉都水有長
丞而官無不備此其所以能饒裕也東南
之地古稱荒服厥土塗泥厥賦下上春秋

本之固，寧不有賴於是歟？請言其槩。夫井田之制，始於商而成於周。有阡陌以定其經界，有溝澮以時其畜洩。古公疆理於岐周，曾孫疆理於原隰，皆是事也。江漢以北，平衍之地，田皆井畫而無廢地，民皆授田而無惰農。先王養民之大政，固莫有過於此者。秦人始廢井田，而先王之法壞矣。然而力於耕桑，地無遺利；頭會箕斂，賦無遺法。而用事之臣各効其能，如鄭國鑿渠於秦，而畆收一鍾；李氷開渠於蜀，而沃野千里。矧井田阡陌雖開，而甽澮距川之法猶有存者，此其所以益富強也。

Field paths established its boundaries, and ditches and channels allowed water to be retained and released at the proper times. Gugong’s demarcation of the lands at Qizhou and the great-grandson’s demarcation of the plains and lowlands were both instances of this work. On the broad, level lands north of the Yangzi and Han rivers, all fields were laid out in well-field grids, leaving no land unused; all the people received fields, leaving no farmers idle. Among the great measures by which the former kings nourished the people, surely none surpassed this. The people of Qin first abolished the well-field system, and the former kings’ institutions fell into ruin. Nevertheless, they exerted themselves in plowing and sericulture, leaving no benefit of the land untapped; they levied taxes by counting heads and collected them by the basketful, leaving no method of taxation unused. The ministers in power each exercised their abilities. Zheng Guo, for example, dug a canal in Qin, so that each mu yielded one zhong of grain; Li Bing opened a canal in Shu, creating fertile countryside extending a thousand li. Moreover, although the well-field boundaries had been broken open, some of the methods for connecting field ditches and channels to rivers still survived. This was how Qin became increasingly wealthy and powerful.
When the Han arose, although it inherited Qin’s arrangements, one year it remitted the land tax, concerned above all lest farming suffer; the next year it encouraged agriculture and sericulture, intent above all on attending to the fundamental occupation. Ministers in power competed in advocating waterworks. Ni Kuan, for example, dug the Six Auxiliary Canals, enriching even the high-lying lands; Lord Bai excavated the Chiyang tract [?], ensuring supplies for the capital. Furthermore, at that time the Waterways and Parks administration had a chief commandant, and the Waterways administration had chiefs and assistants: no official posts were lacking. This was how the Han achieved abundance.

都金陵人物漸蕃開墾益至作陂塘以資
灌溉化荒瘠而為沃壤其財賦始盛自宋

泛溢變沮洳而為良田其財賦益增迨及
我
朝經費全仰於東南矣而西北之賦什不及
一豈獨不能富國而已一遇旱澇每遣廷
臣發內帑以賑貸而猶不免於轉徙何地
===
利之豐嗇財賦之加損古今不同如是邪
噫有由然矣盖先王之制豈不愛膏腴之
地而棄為無用之溝洫誠以所棄者小而
所利者大也今去秦漢千百年中原之地
陵谷變遷九河遺跡尚失其八况區區之
溝洫乎以故澇則千里滔天旱則四郊赤
地雖有人力將何所施邪以愚言之井田
之制固未易以卒復溝洫之政則不可以

噫有由然矣蓋先王之制豈不愛膏腴之

不興必如前代之興水利治之者非一官
punctuated:
之時，介在吴楚；兩漢之際，未暇經營。自吴都金陵，人物漸蕃，開墾益至，作陂塘以資灌溉，化荒瘠而為沃壤，其財賦始盛。自宋遷臨安，農政益舉，播植益勤，築隄防以障泛溢，變沮洳而為良田，其財賦益增。迨及我朝，經費全仰於東南矣，而西北之賦什不及一。豈獨不能富國而已？一遇旱澇，每遣廷臣發內帑以賑貸，而猶不免於轉徙。何地利之豐嗇、財賦之加損，古今不同如是邪？
噫！有由然矣。盖先王之制，豈不愛膏腴之地，而棄為無用之溝洫？誠以所棄者小，而所利者大也。今去秦漢千百年，中原之地，陵谷變遷，九河遺跡尚失其八，况區區之溝洫乎？以故澇則千里滔天，旱則四郊赤地，雖有人力，將何所施邪？以愚言之，井田之制固未易以卒復，溝洫之政則不可以不興。必如前代之興水利，治之者非一官，
translation_en:
…in that period, it lay between Wu and Chu; during the two Han dynasties, there had been no opportunity to develop it. Once Wu established its capital at Jinling, the population and resources gradually increased, and reclamation became more extensive. Reservoirs and ponds were constructed to provide irrigation, transforming barren land into fertile soil, and its tax revenues began to flourish. After the Song moved its capital to Lin’an, agricultural administration was further promoted and planting pursued more diligently. Dikes were built to contain flooding, turning marshes into productive fields, and its tax revenues increased still further. By the time of our dynasty, government expenditure had come to depend entirely upon the southeast, while the tax revenues of the northwest amounted to less than one-tenth as much. Yet is its failure to enrich the state the only problem? Whenever drought or flooding occurs, court officials are dispatched to distribute relief and loans from the imperial treasury, but even then the people cannot avoid displacement. Why do the abundance or scarcity of the land’s resources and the rise or fall of tax revenues differ so greatly between ancient times and today?
Alas! There is a reason for this. In the institutions of the former kings, was it because they did not value fertile land that they set it aside for seemingly useless drainage channels? Truly, it was because what they relinquished was small, while the benefits were great. Now, many centuries have passed since the Qin and Han. In the Central Plain, hills and valleys have shifted; even the traces of eight of the nine river channels have been lost. How much more must this be true of the minor drainage channels! Consequently, when flooding occurs, waters rise to the heavens for a thousand li; when drought occurs, the countryside in every direction becomes parched earth. Even with human labor available, where could it be applied? In my humble opinion, although the well-field system certainly cannot readily be restored all at once, the administration of drainage channels must be revived. We must follow earlier dynasties in developing water management, with its administration entrusted to more than a single official…

punctuated:
領之者非一人，不計地利之廣狹，不論費役之多寡，以盡心於溝洫河渠之間，而溝必因水勢，防必因地勢，旱澇必因時而畜洩，則旱也，潢潦舊德，可轉枯槁為大有；澇也，堤防奏功，可拯墊溺於安居。而又得知水利者如兒寬輩，循行阡陌者如召信臣之流，以為守令，則民力無不盡，地利無或遺矣。今日北方之事，莫有急於此者，豈可憚勞費而不為，而徒諉之氣數哉？雖然，天下之民，均之赤子也。東南民力亦竭矣，獨不可念乎？寬恤之令，可間一舉行也；無名之征，可間一停止也。寬其力於安平之時，得其資於有事之日，此亦所當留意者。執事幸勿專以西北為言。

第五問
張詡

同考試官主事楊批：考論古人之得失，區畫今日之利宜，卓卓有見，豈可以老生之談目之？
translation_en:
…nor should its direction rest with a single person. Regardless of the extent of the land to be benefited or the expense and labor required, every effort should be devoted to drainage ditches, rivers, and canals. Ditches must follow the flow of water, and embankments must suit the terrain; water must be stored or released as circumstances require in drought or flood. Then, in drought, pooled waters can provide their accustomed benefits [?], turning withered crops into an abundant harvest; in flood, effective embankments can rescue people from inundation and drowning and restore them to secure homes. Moreover, if men versed in water management like Ni Kuan, and men who make inspection tours through the fields like Shao Xinchen, are appointed prefects and county magistrates, the people's strength will be fully employed and none of the land's potential benefits will be neglected. No matter in the north today is more urgent than this. How could we shrink from the labor and expense, leave it undone, and merely blame the workings of fate?

Nevertheless, the people throughout the realm are all equally the ruler's children. The strength of the people in the southeast is also exhausted. Can they alone be denied consideration? Orders granting relief might be implemented from time to time, and levies without legitimate grounds might occasionally be suspended. Spare their strength in times of peace, and obtain their resources when need arises: this too deserves attention. I respectfully ask you not to speak exclusively of the northwest.

Fifth Question
Zhang Xu

Comment by Associate Examiner Yang, Secretary: He examines and assesses the successes and failures of the ancients and lays out beneficial and appropriate measures for the present day. His insights are outstanding. How could this be regarded as the commonplace talk of an old scholar?

translation_en:
Associate Examiner Yang, Junior Compiler, comments: Selecting commanders and training soldiers to prepare against attack, and taking the governance of Yu and Zhou as the model—this is indeed [?] the best policy for resisting the Rong, demonstrably practicable. Only a thoroughly learned Confucian could have expressed this. I record it in anticipation of its adoption by His Sagacious Majesty.

Associate Examiner Wu, Senior Compiler, comments: An undertaking succeeds only when the right person is found for it. How much more so with military affairs, among the greatest of undertakings! This policy essay places its emphasis here, and is entirely correct to do so. As for adapting to circumstances and responding to changes so that the enemy cannot escape the compass of our strategies, that assuredly depends upon the person entrusted with the task.

Associate Examiner Wang, Expositor, comments: Repelling external enemies rests upon good internal government: this essay has grasped that principle. As for present measures that should be abolished or implemented, it examines them from every angle, virtually exhausting the subject. Are you perhaps the one whom the ancients described as inexhaustible when called upon to express himself? Ah! I know that you have long turned these matters over in your mind.

Examiner Liu, Secretariat Supervisor of the Heir Apparent, comments: He sets out the successes and failures of present policies for resisting the Rong and proposes ways to address them, all well suited to the actual circumstances. He is evidently a scholar of talent and discernment.

Examiner Peng, Academician, comments: Though these may be called the conventional remarks of a student of the Classics, anyone capable of discussing them in this way must have aspirations of his own.

Those skilled at resisting the Rong should restrain military force in peaceful times and bring it vigorously into action in times of trouble. For the troubles that the Rong and Di cause the Central Kingdom cannot be entirely avoided …

translation_en:
…military preparedness certainly must not be relaxed, yet neither must military force be used recklessly. To relax it is to sink into complacent pursuit of peace, leaving one unable to overawe the Rong and Di; to use it recklessly is to indulge in grandiose ambitions, perhaps even to the point of harming the Central Realm. Thus, when they withdraw, do not pursue them; when they come, be prepared. Restrain or deploy force as circumstances require: this is the proper course. Allow me to elaborate.

The presence of the Rong and Di alongside the Central Realm is like the presence of petty men alongside gentlemen. A gentleman cannot eliminate all petty men, but relies on giving them no grounds to insult him. A true king cannot eliminate all the Rong and Di, but relies on giving them no grounds to insult him. Thus, the military might at our disposal should indeed be prepared in times of peace and employed in times of trouble.

In the age of Youyu, the Sanmiao once relied on their strong defenses. Since they merely relied on those defenses, an expedition against them could be deferred. Emperor Shun therefore did not campaign against them, but had dancers perform with shields and feather plumes between the two stairways. In the Zhou period, the Xianyun once invaded the realm. Since they had already invaded, could an attack on them be deferred? King Xuan therefore resolved to attack and dispatched ten great war chariots. Zhou used force, whereas Youyu did not. Although their policies appear different, in essence they were dictated by the circumstances of their times.

As for Emperor Wu of Han and Emperor Taizong of Tang, one swept away the barbarians of the four quarters and extended his territory a thousand li; the other destroyed the Hu foes, his armies suffering neither defeat nor rout. Yet, as shown by the edict of Luntai and the expedition against Liao, in their later years they too regretted their actions. This departed from the former kings’ rule of not pursuing those who withdraw. Could they escape criticism for reckless use of force? As for the Zhao house’s Song dynasty, it began as a neighbor of…

text:
于契丹終逼於女真今日講和好明日講
和好今年輸幾十萬明年輸幾百萬或僅
結為兄弟之國或又降為叔姪之稱竟不
免靖康之北狩紹興之南遷當時何以自
立邪其視先王来則有備之法缺如也豈
能逭偷安之誚乎迨我
聖祖驅逐胡元肅清海宇復自古帝王之土地
而疆理之取自古帝王之人民而冠裳之
其功之大何如哉然而百餘年来承平日
===

中國百分之一而疆塲被擾亦不能不廑
九重之慮也考之今日要害之地非不守烽
堠之警非不嚴撻伐之威非不張俘馘之

旋羽檄隨至揆厥所自盖由邊將不得其

punctuated: 于契丹，終逼於女真。今日講和好，明日講和好；今年輸幾十萬，明年輸幾百萬。或僅結為兄弟之國，或又降為叔姪之稱，竟不免靖康之北狩、紹興之南遷。當時何以自立邪？其視先王来則有備之法，缺如也，豈能逭偷安之誚乎？迨我聖祖驅逐胡元，肅清海宇，復自古帝王之土地而疆理之，取自古帝王之人民而冠裳之，其功之大何如哉！然而百餘年来，承平日久，殘虜出沒，為我邊患。計其眾，雖不能當中國百分之一，而疆塲被擾，亦不能不廑九重之慮也。考之今日，要害之地非不守，烽堠之警非不嚴，撻伐之威非不張，俘馘之捷非不奏，然而竟未能使之遠遁。麾旄甫旋，羽檄隨至。揆厥所自，盖由邊將不得其人故爾。生事者弋自宿之鳥，刳涸轍之鱗，以為勞；卒然有警，則按兵觀望，或臨機退縮，坐視其至而莫敢膺其鋒，徐待其去而
translation_en:
…with the Khitan, and in the end was hard pressed by the Jurchen. Today it negotiated peace and friendship; tomorrow it negotiated peace and friendship. This year it remitted several hundred thousand; next year, several million. Sometimes it secured only a relationship of brother states; sometimes it was further reduced to the designation of uncle and nephew. In the end, it could not avert the emperors’ enforced “northern journey” during the Jingkang era or the southward relocation during the Shaoxing era. How could it maintain its independence under such circumstances? Measured against the former kings’ principle of being prepared when the enemy comes, it was deficient. How could it escape the reproach of seeking ease at any price?

Then our sagely founder drove out the alien Yuan, pacified all within the seas, recovered and established boundaries over the lands held by emperors and kings since antiquity, and brought their people once more into the civilized order of caps and robes. How great was his achievement! Yet, with more than a hundred years of enduring peace, the remaining barbarians have appeared and disappeared, causing trouble on our borders. Although their numbers cannot amount to even one hundredth of China’s population, their disturbances along the frontier cannot but trouble His Majesty.

Examining present conditions, strategically vital places are indeed defended, beacon-post vigilance is indeed strict, the might of punitive expeditions is indeed displayed, and victories measured in captives and severed ears are indeed reported. Yet we have never succeeded in driving them far away. Scarcely have our command banners returned when urgent military dispatches arrive in their wake. Considering the source of this, it is surely because the frontier commands have not been entrusted to the right men. Those who provoke trouble shoot at birds settled on their roosts and gut fish stranded in dried-up cart ruts, claiming these as meritorious deeds. When an alarm suddenly comes, however, they hold their troops back and wait to see what happens, or shrink back at the critical moment. They sit watching the enemy advance, none daring to face the brunt of the attack, and leisurely wait for the enemy to depart, and…

僅能曵其尾所傷既多則深為蔽匿以避
誅所得雖少則强為張大以邀賞非惟不
足以禦其侮而適足以損吾威釀成此患
殆非一日兹欲致金帛以結之則吾豈趙
宋之委靡矧狼貪豕欲丘壑難填金帛可
恃乎抑窮兵力以追之則吾豈漢唐之虛
夸矧鴟張鼠竄顯伏不常兵力可久乎以
諸生之愚見為
明時之良策莫若慎擇守臣而隨時浮沉者
===

托方叔之賢運籌藉子房之略守充國萬
全之謀養李牧必勝之銳車馬以修器械

王也則戢吾之武而懷徠之以恩如虞之
格有苗不咎其既往也及其伺間而入寇

translation_en:
…can only drag at their tails as they retreat. When our casualties are numerous, the commanders carefully conceal them to escape punishment; when their gains are meager, they exaggerate them to seek rewards. Not only do they fail to resist the enemy’s affronts, they actually diminish our prestige. This calamity has surely been long in the making. If we now seek to offer gold and silk to secure their friendship, should we succumb to the weakness of the Zhao house’s Song dynasty? Moreover, their wolfish greed and swinish appetites are ravines impossible to fill: can gold and silk be relied upon? Or, if we exhaust our military strength in pursuing them, should we indulge in the empty vainglory of the Han and Tang? Moreover, they swagger like owls and scurry away like rats, now appearing and now hiding without constancy: can military exertion be sustained indefinitely?
In this student’s humble view, the best policy for this enlightened age is to choose frontier officials carefully, invariably dismissing those who drift with the times; and to seek distinguished generals with discernment, invariably punishing the greedy, incompetent, base, and cowardly. Entrust our defense to men as worthy as Fang Shu, and our strategic planning to men with the resourcefulness of Zifang. Adhere to Chongguo’s plans for complete security, and nurture the fighting vigor with which Li Mu assured victory. Put chariots and horses in good order, prepare weapons and equipment, train the troops, and make grain supplies abundant. When they change their outward bearing [?] and come to acknowledge our sovereign, let us restrain our arms and win them over through kindness, as the ruler of Yu brought the Youmiao to submission, without reproaching them for their past offenses. When they watch for an opening and invade, let us rouse our forces and overawe them with our might, as Zhou attacked the Xianyun, without slighting them as unworthy opponents. title: 成化二十年會試錄
text:
威不可犯其肯終為我邊陲患哉此雖儒
生之常談而今日備禦之策誠不能外是
也雖然書曰無怠無荒四夷來王是則所
以治內者又不專在於威武也愚敢以是
為終篇獻

生之常談而今日備禦之策誠不能外是
也雖然書曰無怠無荒四夷來王是則所
以治内者又不專在於威武也愚敢以是

punctuated: 威不可犯，其肯終為我邊陲患哉？此雖儒生之常談，而今日備禦之策，誠不能外是也。雖然，《書》曰：「無怠無荒，四夷來王。」是則所以治內者，又不專在於威武也。愚敢以是為終篇獻。
translation_en: …that our might cannot be defied. Would they then persist in bringing trouble to our frontiers? Though these are the commonplace observations of a Confucian scholar, present-day measures for defense truly cannot depart from them. Nevertheless, the Book of Documents says: “Be neither indolent nor neglectful, and the peoples of the four quarters will come to acknowledge your kingship.” Thus, governing within the realm does not depend exclusively on military might. I humbly venture to offer this thought in closing.

會試錄後序

成化甲辰春二月，當取士之期，士之貢于鄉者畢會禮部，尚書臣洪謨等以聞。上命臣華、臣健為考試官，典司去取。臣等被命惟謹，遂以是月甲子入院，至于甲申，旬再浹而畢，拔取三百人，蓋制數也。

故事，試必有錄，具載中式者氏名及諸執事，與其文之尤純者以獻。臣健當序于其後。竊惟自鄉舉里選之法不行，凡君天下
translation_en:
Postface to the Record of the Metropolitan Examination

In the second month of spring in the jiachen year of Chenghua (1484), when the time came to select men for office, all the scholars recommended from the provinces assembled at the Ministry of Rites. Your servant Hong Mo, Minister of Rites, and the others reported this to the throne. His Majesty appointed your servants Hua and Jian as Examiners, charged with deciding whom to reject and whom to select. We reverently received the command and entered the examination compound on the jiazi day of that month. By the jiashen day, after two ten-day periods, the work was complete. We selected three hundred men, the quota prescribed by imperial decree.

According to established practice, every examination must have a record, fully listing the names of successful candidates and all the officials who served, together with the most exemplary of the candidates’ compositions, for presentation to the throne. It fell to your servant Jian to write the postface. I humbly reflect that, since the system of recommending men from the districts and selecting them from the villages ceased to be practiced, all those who rule the realm…

translation_en:
…those who rule the realm have, in selecting men for service, generally relied on empty words alone. If they attend to empty words without reaching actual conduct, how can they obtain worthy men? Yet when your servant has considered this matter, he has found grounds for drawing distinctions. The Sui and Tang selected men entirely through verse and rhapsodies. Although the Song sometimes also used classical learning, they were further misled by Wang’s New Interpretations of the Classics, which differed little from verse and rhapsodies. To compose literary works without adhering wholly to principle is surely empty verbiage at its worst. This is why the habits of scholars and the achievements of government under those several dynasties ultimately failed to match antiquity.
The sagely progenitors and divine ancestors of our august Ming established institutions and bequeathed instructions, taking as their basis the Six Classics edited and transmitted by Confucius, and what Yan Hui, Zeng Shen, Zisi, and Mencius received and passed down, and Zhou and Cheng …

punctuated: 張朱所講明之實理，乃斯人修身齊家治國平天下之具，悉取而立之學官，為養士取士之式，規摹固已宏遠矣。而聖聖相承，及今日我皇上，尤增光而廓大之。比者，以列聖之造士，經學雖備，而史學猶有闕焉，特命儒臣校訂朱子《通鑑綱目》，又編纂宋元二史以續之，使天下學者本之經以窮其理，參之史以考其事，所以為修齊治平之具，盖無不至。是以百餘年来，士習益正，治效益
translation_en: …the substantive principles elucidated by Zhang and Zhu are the means by which people cultivate themselves, bring order to their families, govern the state, and bring peace to the realm. All were adopted and established in the official schools as standards for educating and selecting scholars. The scope of this undertaking was already expansive and far-reaching. Sage sovereign succeeded sage sovereign, down to our present Emperor, who has further enhanced and broadened it. Recently, considering that the successive sage sovereigns’ education of scholars was comprehensive in classical learning but still deficient in historical learning, he specially commanded Confucian court officials to collate and revise Master Zhu’s Outline and Details of the Comprehensive Mirror (Tongjian gangmu), and also to compile histories of the Song and Yuan dynasties to continue it. Thus scholars throughout the realm could take the Classics as their foundation in fully investigating principles and consult the histories to examine events. The means provided for cultivating oneself, ordering the family, governing the state, and bringing peace to the realm were thereby complete in every respect. Hence, over the past hundred years and more, scholars’ habits have become increasingly upright, and the achievements of government increasingly…

title: 成化二十年會試錄
text:
隆而人材之出彬彬然無愧
于古其視隋唐而下之制專
務空言而不及實行者不可
同日而語矣諸士子荷
造就之恩茲既以純理之言登
名選列幸孰大焉然亦不可
徒自幸宜思所以報稱也是
===
故凡聖賢所言之實理既究
知之必務修之身為實德措
之家國天下為實行使他日
或為名臣或為大儒無一行
而不本于是斯誠不負
聖天子之造就不負今日之科目
矣其或但取聖賢言論之餘

===
故凡聖賢所言之實理既究
知之必務修之身為實德措
之家國天下為實行使他日
或為名臣或為大儒無一行
而不本于是斯誠不負
聖天子之造就不負今日之科目
矣其或但取聖賢言論之餘
punctuated:
隆，而人材之出彬彬然，無愧于古。其視隋唐而下之制，專務空言而不及實行者，不可同日而語矣。諸士子荷造就之恩，茲既以純理之言登名選列，幸孰大焉？然亦不可徒自幸，宜思所以報稱也。

是故，凡聖賢所言之實理，既究知之，必務修之身為實德，措之家國天下為實行，使他日或為名臣，或為大儒，無一行而不本于是。斯誠不負聖天子之造就，不負今日之科目矣。其或但取聖賢言論之餘
translation_en:
…has flourished, while men of talent have emerged in cultivated abundance, worthy of comparison with the ancients. Compared with the institutions of the Sui and Tang dynasties and later ages, which devoted themselves exclusively to empty words without extending to actual conduct, the present system cannot be spoken of in the same breath. You candidates have received the gracious benefit of this cultivation, and now, through words expressing pure principle, your names have entered the ranks of those selected. What greater good fortune could there be? Yet you must not merely congratulate yourselves; you should consider how to repay this favor fittingly.

Thus, once you have thoroughly understood the substantive principles expressed by the sages and worthies, you must strive to cultivate them in your own persons as genuine virtue and apply them to family, state, and all under Heaven as actual practice. Then, whether you become eminent ministers or great Confucian scholars in days to come, not a single action will fail to be grounded in these principles. In this way you will truly live up to the sage Son of Heaven’s cultivation of you and to the examination distinction you have attained today. Should any of you merely take the remnants of the sages’ and worthies’ words…

title: 成化二十年會試錄
text:

甘與隋唐而下空言之士伍
焉則非今日主司所望於諸
士子也盍相與勉之
奉政大夫脩正庶尹左春坊

…cutting and patching them together into literary compositions to angle for fame and profit, willingly joining the ranks of men of empty words from the Sui and Tang dynasties onward—this is not what those presiding over the examination today expect of you candidates. Why not encourage one another in this endeavor?
Preface respectfully composed by Liu Jian, Grand Master for Government Service, Administrator of Rectitude (xiuzheng shuyin) [?], and Left Supervisor of Instruction in the Left Secretariat of the Heir Apparent.
